eng-p001.title: The Gaps in the Road
eng-p001.text:
Drivers crossing a long bridge sometimes feel a faint bump every few hundred metres and assume the road has been badly laid. In fact, those metal strips with teeth like a comb are placed there on purpose. They are expansion joints, and without them the bridge would slowly tear itself apart.

Almost every solid grows a little longer when it warms and shrinks when it cools. For a pencil the change is far too small to notice, but a steel or concrete deck several hundred metres long can lengthen by many centimetres between a cold winter night and a blazing summer afternoon. If both ends of the deck were fixed rigidly to the banks, the material would have nowhere to go. In the heat it would push against its supports with enormous force; in the cold it would pull on them. Over the years, this repeated strain would crack the concrete and loosen the bolts.

The joint solves the problem by leaving a deliberate gap that can open and close. Its interlocking teeth let wheels roll smoothly across while the two sections slide towards or away from each other. Engineers calculate the widest gap the local climate could demand and then add a margin, because a joint that is too narrow is almost worse than none at all. So the next time a tyre thumps over one, remember that the bump is the sound of a bridge being allowed to breathe.

eng-p002.title: Why Builders Water Hard Concrete
eng-p002.text:
On building sites across Pakistan, labourers can be seen spraying water over a freshly laid concrete roof, sometimes for a week or more, even though the slab already looks hard. To a passer-by this seems pointless. Surely water is what concrete needs to lose in order to dry?

The confusion comes from the way we talk about it. Concrete does not harden by drying, as mud or paint does. It hardens through a chemical reaction between cement and water, called hydration, in which tiny crystals grow and knit the sand and stones together. This reaction is fastest in the first few days but continues for weeks, and it can only go on while water is present inside the mix. If the surface dries out too early, especially under a fierce summer sun, hydration near the top stops before the crystals have fully formed. The result is a weak, dusty skin that may crack within months.

Keeping concrete damp, a practice known as curing, therefore does not soften it; it allows it to reach the strength it was designed for. Builders cover slabs with wet sacking, hold shallow pools of water on flat roofs, or spray them several times a day. None of this is glamorous, and on a busy site it is often the first task to be skipped. Yet a careful engineer will tell you that the week after pouring matters almost as much as the pour itself.

eng-p003.title: Sun or Wind for Darband?
eng-p003.text:
When the council of a small hill village called Darband decided to generate its own electricity, the debate quickly narrowed to two choices: a field of solar panels or a pair of wind turbines on the ridge above the houses. Both rely on free fuel and both produce no smoke, but they behave very differently.

Solar panels are simple. They have no moving parts, need little more than an occasional wash, and their output is easy to predict: strong at noon, weaker on cloudy days, and nothing at all after dark. Turbines are more temperamental. A good site can produce power around the clock, including on winter nights when the village needs light most, but the wind rises and falls without warning, and the gearboxes and blades need skilled care that a remote village may struggle to find.

In the end, the engineer advising the council, a patient woman named Farah Qureshi, refused to declare a winner. The ridge, she pointed out, was windiest in exactly the months when the valley was most often under cloud. Panels and turbines, in other words, tended to fall short at different times. Her recommendation was a modest mix of the two, with a bank of batteries to cover the quiet hours. It was not the dramatic answer some councillors had hoped for, but it was the one that kept the lights on.

eng-p004.title: Counting the Seconds
eng-p004.text:
Children in many parts of Pakistan learn a simple trick during the monsoon: when lightning flashes, count the seconds until the thunder arrives. The longer the count, the further away the storm. The trick works because light and sound, though they are produced at the same instant, travel at wildly different speeds.

Light crosses the distance from a lightning bolt to an observer almost instantly; for any storm you could see, the delay is far too short for a human to notice. Sound is a different matter. It moves as a wave of squeezed and stretched air, passed from one layer of molecules to the next, and covers roughly one kilometre in three seconds. A count of nine therefore means the bolt struck about three kilometres away.

The same gap explains a familiar puzzle at cricket grounds. A spectator seated far from the pitch sees the bat strike the ball a moment before he hears the crack, as if the picture and the sound had slipped apart. Nothing is wrong with his ears; the sound is simply still on its way.

The rule has its limits. Wind and temperature nudge the speed of sound up or down a little, and a long, rolling peal of thunder makes it hard to know when to stop counting. But as a rough guide it is remarkably reliable, and it has the rare virtue of turning a frightening moment into a small piece of arithmetic.

eng-p005.title: A World Built from Two Symbols
eng-p005.text:
Inside every computer, from a giant server to the phone in your pocket, information is stored using only two states. A tiny switch in the memory is either on or off, and engineers write these two states as 1 and 0. Everything the machine handles, whether a photograph, a song or a message to a friend, must first be turned into long strings of these binary digits, or bits.

It may seem strange to limit a powerful machine to just two symbols when we ourselves count with ten. The reason is reliability. An electronic switch that only has to be clearly on or clearly off can tolerate a good deal of electrical noise; a small wobble in voltage will not change a 1 into a 0. A switch asked to hold ten different levels would have to tell them apart precisely, and the slightest disturbance could turn a 7 into an 8. Two states, in short, are hard to confuse.

What each switch lacks in range, the system makes up in sheer quantity. A single bit can say only yes or no, but eight bits together, called a byte, can form 256 different patterns, enough to give every letter, digit and punctuation mark its own code. Modern memory chips hold billions of such switches, packed so closely that thousands of books would fit on a chip smaller than a fingernail. The computer's apparent cleverness, then, rests on a humble foundation: an enormous number of very simple choices.

eng-p006.title: Cooler Homes Without Machines
eng-p006.text:
In cities such as Multan and Jacobabad, summer afternoons can make a concrete house feel like an oven long after sunset. The flat roof absorbs heat all day and releases it into the rooms at night, just when families are trying to sleep. Air conditioners help, but they are expensive to run, they strain the electricity supply during the hottest hours, and they pump yet more heat into the street outside.

Some of the most effective remedies are surprisingly cheap. The simplest is to paint the roof white or cover it with a light-coloured coating. Dark surfaces soak up most of the sunlight that falls on them, while white ones reflect much of it back into the sky, so a whitened roof stays noticeably cooler. Shade helps too: a creeper on a sunny wall or a row of trees along a lane keeps the sun off the bricks before it can warm them.

Older buildings offer lessons as well. Traditional houses in the region often had thick walls, small windows on the sunny side and a courtyard that drew cooler air through the rooms in the evening. Builders abandoned many of these features when concrete became fashionable, partly because they took up space and partly because they looked old-fashioned.

None of these measures will make a June afternoon pleasant. But taken together, they can lower indoor temperatures enough to let people sleep, and let the air conditioner, where there is one, work less hard.

eng-p007.title: Built to Be Mended
eng-p007.text:
My grandfather's ceiling fan ran for more than thirty years. When it faltered, a mechanic in the bazaar opened it with an ordinary screwdriver, replaced a worn bearing and sent it home the same afternoon. Many of the machines we buy today could not survive such treatment. Their cases are glued rather than screwed shut, their parts are sold only to approved workshops, and a fault in one small component often means throwing away the whole device.

Manufacturers defend these choices. Glued cases, they say, keep out dust and water, and a sealed design can be thinner and lighter. Some of this is true. But a product that cannot be opened is also a product that must be replaced, and replacement is far more profitable than repair. Customers pay twice, and the discarded machines pile up as electronic waste that few places are equipped to handle safely.

Engineers should treat repairability as a basic requirement, in the same way that they already treat safety. That need not mean bulky or old-fashioned products. It means using standard screws, making spare parts and repair guides available, and arranging components so that the ones most likely to wear out can be reached easily. These are decisions made at the drawing board, and they cost little if taken early.

A machine that can be mended is not a step backwards. It is a sign that its makers respected both the people who bought it and the world that will one day have to absorb it.

eng-p008.title: Fighting Sound with Sound
eng-p008.text:
Anyone who has sat through a long bus journey knows the low, endless drone of the engine. Ordinary earphones can only fight it by playing music louder, which tires the ears. Noise-cancelling headphones take a cleverer approach: they fight sound with sound.

Sound is a pattern of pressure in the air, rising and falling like a wave on water. Two waves that meet can combine. If the peaks of one line up with the peaks of the other, they reinforce each other and the sound grows louder. If, instead, the peaks of one meet the troughs of the other, they cancel out, and the result can be close to silence.

Noise-cancelling headphones exploit this second case. A small microphone on the outside of each ear cup listens to the surrounding noise. A chip inside then produces a copy of that wave turned upside down, so that every rise becomes a fall, and plays it through the speaker along with the music. When the two meet inside the ear, much of the drone disappears.

The trick has an important weakness. It works best on steady, low sounds, such as engines and air-conditioning units, which change slowly enough for the chip to keep pace. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, like a baby crying or a door slamming, are harder to predict, so they slip through. For these, the padding of the ear cups, which simply blocks sound, does most of the work.

eng-p009.title: Copper or Aluminium?
eng-p009.text:
Look inside the wall of a house and you will usually find copper wiring; look up at the high-voltage lines strung between tall towers and you will usually be looking at aluminium. Both metals carry electricity well, so why do engineers choose differently in the two places?

Copper is the better conductor of the two. A copper wire offers less resistance to the current than an aluminium wire of the same thickness, so it wastes less energy as heat. It is also tough and can be bent many times without cracking, which matters in a house, where wires are pulled through narrow pipes and twisted around switches. Its drawbacks are weight and cost: it is heavy, and it is considerably more expensive.

Aluminium turns these drawbacks into its strengths. It is only about a third as heavy as copper and much cheaper. To carry the same current, an aluminium cable must be made thicker, but even then it weighs less than its copper equivalent. Over long distances, where cables hang for hundreds of metres between towers, this lightness is decisive: lighter cables need fewer and less massive towers. Inside a house, however, aluminium's softness can be a danger. Its joints may loosen over time, overheat and, in the worst cases, start a fire.

Neither metal, then, is simply better than the other. Each is the right answer to a different question.

eng-p010.title: The Machine That Moves Heat
eng-p010.text:
A refrigerator seems to make cold, but it does nothing of the kind. Cold is not a substance that can be produced; it is simply the absence of heat. What a refrigerator actually does is move heat, collecting it from the food inside and releasing it into the kitchen. That is why the back of a working fridge feels warm.

The job is done by a special fluid called a refrigerant, which circulates endlessly through a loop of pipes. Inside the cabinet, the refrigerant is allowed to expand to a low pressure, where it evaporates and becomes a gas. Evaporation needs energy, and the fluid takes that energy from its surroundings, in the same way that sweat cools your skin as it dries. The air and food inside the fridge grow colder.

The gas is then drawn into the compressor, the humming motor near the bottom of the machine, which squeezes it hard. Squeezing a gas heats it, so the refrigerant leaves the compressor hotter than the kitchen air. It flows through a grid of thin pipes on the outside of the fridge, gives up its heat to the room, and turns back into a liquid, ready to begin the circuit again.

This explains a common mistake. People sometimes leave a fridge door open on a hot day, hoping to cool the kitchen. The machine works harder, but the room does not get cooler, because the heat it pulls from the open cabinet is released again behind it, along with extra heat from its own motor.

eng-p011.title: The Tunnels That Drink from Hills
eng-p011.text:
In the dry valleys of Balochistan, long before electric pumps, farmers built the karez: a gently sloping tunnel that carries groundwater from the foot of a hill to fields lying lower down. A line of vertical shafts, dug every few dozen metres, marks its route on the surface. Workers used these shafts to lower themselves into the tunnel and to haul out the earth they removed.

The design is cleverer than it looks. Because the channel runs underground, very little water is lost to the fierce summer sun, which would evaporate much of the flow in an open canal. And because it relies only on gravity, a karez needs no fuel; it keeps delivering water as long as the aquifer that feeds it is replenished by rain and snow in the hills.

That same dependence is now its weakness. In many villages, tube wells sunk nearby draw water from the same aquifer far faster than it can recover. As the water table falls below the level of the tunnel, the karez simply runs dry, and the families who once shared its flow by an agreed rota of hours lose a supply that served them for generations. Some communities have responded by limiting new wells near their karez, recognising that an old system can survive only if the ground beneath it is treated as a shared account rather than a private one.

eng-p012.title: When Ice Lakes Burst
eng-p012.text:
High in the mountains of northern Pakistan, warmer summers are melting glaciers faster than before. The meltwater often collects behind walls of loose rock and ice that a glacier pushed forward long ago, forming lakes that can swell quietly for years. If such a wall gives way, the lake can empty in hours, sending a torrent of water, mud and boulders down a valley where villages, bridges and terraced fields sit close to the river.

Such floods cannot always be prevented, but their toll can be greatly reduced. In several valleys, sensors now watch the level of the most dangerous lakes and send a signal when the water rises suddenly. Equally important is what happens next, because a warning is useless unless people know where to go. Villagers have therefore practised evacuations, marked safe routes to higher ground and chosen local volunteers who can sound an alarm even if the mobile network fails.

Engineers can also lower a risky lake on purpose, cutting a controlled channel through its wall so that the water drains slowly rather than all at once. None of these measures is glamorous. Yet together they reflect a sensible shift in thinking: rather than waiting for disaster and then rushing in with relief, communities and officials are learning to spend modestly beforehand so that they do not pay dearly afterwards.

eng-p013.title: Why Winter Air Turns Grey
eng-p013.text:
Every winter, people in Lahore and other cities on the plains of Punjab watch the sky change from blue to a dull, choking grey. It is tempting to blame a single culprit, but smog is the product of several sources meeting the wrong kind of weather.

Smoke and fine dust are released throughout the year by vehicles, brick kilns, factories and household fires, and in some seasons by farmers burning the stubble left after a harvest. In summer, much of this pollution is carried away. The ground heats the air just above it, the warm air rises, and the particles are lifted and scattered high into the sky.

Winter reverses this pattern. On cold, still nights the ground loses heat quickly and chills the layer of air closest to it, while a layer of warmer air sits on top like a lid. Because cold air is heavier, it stays put, and the smoke released into it has nowhere to go. Weather scientists call this an inversion. Day after day the trapped particles accumulate, and the fog that forms in the moist air binds with them into a thick, lingering haze.

Understanding this mechanism matters because it shows where relief must come from. The weather cannot be changed, so the only lever left is the amount of smoke put into the air in the first place, especially during the weeks when inversions are most common.

eng-p014.title: When Water Turns the Soil White
eng-p014.text:
Driving through parts of the Indus plain, a visitor may notice patches of field that glitter white in the sun, as if dusted with frost. The white crust is salt, and where it spreads, wheat and cotton struggle to grow.

The cause lies partly in the very irrigation that made these plains productive. Canal water carries small amounts of dissolved salt. When fields are flooded season after season and the water cannot drain away, the water table creeps up towards the surface. In the heat, moisture rises through the soil and evaporates, leaving its salt behind, and year by year the deposit thickens. Paradoxically, then, too much water can make land as barren as too little.

The remedies are known, though none is quick. Drains laid beneath the fields can lower the water table and carry salty water away. Farmers can level their land so that water spreads evenly instead of pooling in low corners, and use only as much as the crop needs. On land already damaged, some grow salt-tolerant crops or fodder grasses while the soil is slowly flushed clean. Each of these steps costs money or effort at the start, which is why the help of agricultural extension workers, who can show farmers the results on a neighbour's field, often decides whether the steps are taken at all.

eng-p015.title: Counting Trees Is Not Enough
eng-p015.text:
Tree-planting drives have become a familiar sight: officials and schoolchildren posing with saplings, followed by announcements of how many millions have gone into the ground. The enthusiasm is welcome. But a number planted tells us almost nothing about a forest grown, and it is time we judged such campaigns by what is still standing five years later.

A sapling is a fragile thing. Planted in the wrong season, left without water through its first summer, or nibbled by goats, it dies quietly, long after the cameras have gone. The choice of species matters too. Fast-growing foreign trees are popular because they look impressive quickly, yet some drink heavily from scarce groundwater, and others offer little food or shelter to local birds and insects. A native tree may grow more slowly, but it is suited to the soil and climate it was born into.

None of this is an argument against planting. It is an argument for patience and care: choosing species that belong, fencing and watering young trees, and paying local caretakers whose job lasts years rather than an afternoon. A campaign that plants fewer trees but keeps most of them alive has done more for the land than one that plants many and forgets them. Survival, not ceremony, should be the measure of success.

eng-p016.title: My Grandmother's Tin Box
eng-p016.text:
When I was ten, I thought my grandmother, whom we called Nani, was simply stingy. She washed plastic bags and pegged them on the line to dry. She kept a tin box full of buttons cut from shirts too worn to mend, and she turned old dupattas into quilt covers. When I begged for a new pencil box because mine had a cracked lid, she fixed it with a strip of cloth and some glue and handed it back without a word.

Our house in Multan produced so little rubbish that the sweeper once asked my mother, half joking, whether anyone lived there. I was embarrassed. My friends' families bought things, used them and threw them away, and that seemed to me what modern people did.

It was years later, in a university lecture on waste, that I began to see Nani differently. The lecturer showed pictures of rubbish heaps smouldering at the edge of a city and spoke about how much of what we throw away could have been repaired or used again. I thought of the tin box, the patched pencil box and the quilts that had kept three generations warm.

Nani never used words like "sustainability". To her, wasting something was a small failure of respect, both for the thing and for the work that had gone into making it. I still have her tin box, and I open it whenever I am tempted to throw away something that could be mended.

eng-p017.title: Catching the Rain
eng-p017.text:
In many Pakistani cities the same street can suffer from both too much water and too little. During a heavy monsoon shower, rain pours off roofs and roads, overwhelms the drains and floods low-lying lanes within the hour. A few months later, the same households queue for tanker water because their wells and taps have run low.

The two problems are linked. As cities spread, soil that once soaked up rain is sealed under concrete and asphalt. Water that would have seeped slowly into the ground, topping up the aquifer below, instead races into gutters and out of the city. The water table drops, while drains built for a smaller town cannot cope with the sudden rush.

Rainwater harvesting offers a modest but real answer. A house can lead the water from its roof into a storage tank for washing and gardening, or into a recharge well: a shaft filled with layers of gravel and sand that filters the water and lets it sink into the ground. Parks and school playgrounds can be shaped to hold rainwater for a few hours instead of shedding it at once. No single roof will refill an aquifer, of course. But if thousands of buildings did the same, a city could ease its floods and its shortages with one habit, and that seems to me too good a bargain to ignore.

eng-p018.title: Why Cities Stay Hot After Dark
eng-p018.text:
On a summer evening, a family driving back from a village to Faisalabad may feel the difference before they reach home: the city is hotter, and it stays hot long after sunset. Scientists call this effect the urban heat island, and its causes lie in what a city is made of.

Brick, concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight through the day and store its heat. After dark they release it slowly, warming the air around them, so streets that bake at noon are still radiating warmth at midnight. In the countryside, by contrast, fields and trees cool down soon after the sun sets. Plants also cool their surroundings in a less obvious way: they draw water from the soil and release it through their leaves, and the evaporation of that water absorbs heat, much as sweat cools the skin.

A city adds heat of its own, too. Engines, factories and air conditioners all pour warmth into the streets. Ironically, each air conditioner that cools a room pushes hot air outside, making the street a little worse for everyone else.

This explains why shade trees and green spaces are more than decoration. A row of trees along a road blocks the sun before it reaches the pavement and also cools the air through its leaves. A well-planted neighbourhood can therefore feel noticeably cooler than a bare one only a short walk away.

eng-p019.title: The Case for the Mixed Farm
eng-p019.text:
For much of the last century, farming advice pointed in one direction: choose the most profitable crop, plant it over every acre, and feed it with fertiliser and pesticide. On paper the logic is hard to fault. A single crop is simpler to sow, spray and harvest, and a good year can bring a handsome return.

Yet the farmer who relies on one crop has put all his eggs in a single basket. A late frost, a new pest or a fall in the market price can wipe out a year's income at a stroke. The soil suffers as well. The same plant, grown on the same land year after year, draws the same nutrients from it and invites the same pests back each season, so ever more chemicals are needed to keep yields up.

A mixed farm spreads these risks. Wheat might share the land with lentils, which enrich the soil with nitrogen; a few buffaloes turn crop leftovers into milk and manure; a line of trees along the boundary gives fodder, firewood and shade. No single part of such a farm earns as much as the best cash crop in its best year. But the whole is steadier, and the land is in better health at the end of a decade than at the start. For a small farmer, who cannot survive one ruinous season, steadiness is worth more than the chance of a windfall.

eng-p020.title: The Invisible Workers in a Compost Heap
eng-p020.text:
A heap of kitchen peelings, dry leaves and grass clippings left in the corner of a garden does not simply sit there. Within days it begins to warm, and within a few months it has turned into a dark, crumbly material that smells like a forest floor. This change is called composting, and the workers who carry it out are too small to see.

Bacteria and fungi feed on the waste, breaking it down into simpler substances. As they multiply they give off heat, and the centre of a healthy heap can become too hot to touch. Later, as the easily digested material runs out, the heap cools, and larger creatures such as earthworms and beetles move in to finish the job.

These organisms need the right conditions. They need air, which is why a heap is turned from time to time; without it the waste rots slowly and gives off a sour smell. They need moisture, but not so much that the heap becomes soggy. And they need a balance of "greens", such as fresh peelings, which are rich in nitrogen, and "browns", such as dry leaves and cardboard, which supply carbon.

When food waste goes to a landfill instead, it is buried under other rubbish where air cannot reach it. There it decays without oxygen and releases methane, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere. Composting the same waste at home turns a source of pollution into free fertiliser for the soil.

eng-p021.title: Why the Buzz Wins
eng-p021.text:
A phone does not need to ring loudly to win our attention. A single short vibration in a pocket is enough to break the thread of a sentence we are reading or a sum we are solving. Many psychologists believe the reason lies less in the phone itself than in the way it rewards us. Most messages are dull, but now and then one brings good news, a joke from a friend or a word of praise. Because we can never tell which buzz will be the rewarding one, we check every time, much as a visitor at a fair keeps pulling a game's lever in case the next try pays.

The cost of each check is larger than it seems. Glancing at a screen takes only a few seconds, but returning to the original task takes much longer. The mind has to rebuild what it was holding: the argument of the chapter, the step reached in the calculation. Psychologists call this the cost of switching, and it is paid in full every time, however brief the interruption.

This explains why a student who studies for two hours with her phone beside her may achieve less than a friend who studies for one hour with his phone in another room. The first student has not really studied for two hours; she has studied in dozens of short pieces, each begun by picking up where she left off. The remedy is not willpower alone but distance: a phone that is out of reach cannot tug at the sleeve.

eng-p022.title: Read Before You Share
eng-p022.text:
There was a time when a rumour moved at the speed of gossip, from one courtyard to the next. Today it moves at the speed of a thumb. A false report about a poisoned water supply, a fake notice of school closures or a doctored photograph can reach thousands of phones in an afternoon, and by the time it is corrected the damage is done. It is tempting to blame only the people who invent such stories, and they certainly deserve blame. But I want to argue that the rest of us, the ordinary forwarders, carry a share of the responsibility too.

Most of us do not forward a message because we have checked it. We forward it because it alarms us, or because it confirms what we already suspected, or because it came from a cousin we trust. None of these is evidence. A message does not become true by passing through a respectable relative, any more than a counterfeit note becomes genuine by passing through an honest hand.

The habit I am proposing is modest. Before sharing anything that would frighten or anger people, pause for one minute. Ask who first wrote it, whether a known newspaper or official source reports the same thing, and whether the photograph could belong to another place or year. If you cannot answer, do not share. Silence costs nothing; a false alarm can cost a great deal.

eng-p023.title: The Machine in the Corner
eng-p023.text:
Tariq Mehmood had counted cash at the same bank branch in Okara for nineteen years when the machine arrived. It stood in the corner of the hall, grey and patient, and within a month it was doing in seconds what had taken him the better part of a morning: accepting deposits, printing statements and paying out notes without a single miscount. Customers who had once queued at his window now queued at the machine instead, and some of them did not even nod to him as they passed.

For a few weeks he was sure he would be the next thing removed. He came to work early and left late, as if diligence alone could argue his case. Then the manager called him in, not to dismiss him but to ask for his help. Older customers, she said, were frightened of the machine; farmers who had banked there all their lives would not touch it, and some had begun to take their savings elsewhere.

So Tariq became, without any new title, the person who stood beside the machine. He showed a widow how to read her balance on the screen and taught a retired schoolmaster to change his PIN. Slowly he discovered that what customers had valued in him was never really his speed with notes. It was that they knew him, and that he was patient with them. The machine could count; it could not reassure.

eng-p024.title: Two Kinds of Classroom
eng-p024.text:
When schools closed for long periods a few years ago, many students in Pakistan discovered online learning almost overnight. Now that classrooms have reopened, it is worth comparing the two calmly, without the panic of those months.

The strengths of online study are real. A recorded lecture can be paused, replayed and watched at midnight; a student in a small town can hear a teacher from a famous college; a shy learner can type a question she would never ask aloud. For a disciplined student with a good connection, these are large advantages.

The classroom, however, offers things that are harder to see. A teacher standing in a room notices the puzzled face in the third row and explains again before anyone asks. Classmates argue, compare answers and carry each other through difficult weeks. Above all, the fixed timetable does the work of discipline for the student: one does not have to decide every morning whether to study, because the bell decides.

The comparison suggests that the two are not rivals so much as tools for different needs. Online material is best at delivering information; the classroom is best at sustaining effort and catching confusion early. A sensible student will use recorded lessons to revise and to fill gaps, but will not expect a screen to supply the steady push that a room full of people provides.

eng-p025.title: Paying Without Money
eng-p025.text:
Many of the apps on a typical phone cost nothing to download, yet the companies behind them employ thousands of people and earn large profits. The puzzle has a simple answer: the user is paying, but not with money. The payment is information.

Every search, every pause over a video, every place visited with location turned on adds a detail to a profile. One detail on its own says little. Put together, thousands of them can reveal a surprising amount: what a person can afford, what worries them, whether they are about to change jobs or get married. Advertisers will pay well to place their message in front of exactly the right person at exactly the right moment, and such profiles make that possible.

None of this is hidden in the strict sense. It is usually described in the terms and conditions that users accept with a tap. But few people read those pages, and fewer still could say afterwards what they had agreed to. Consent given in this way is real in law but thin in practice.

Understanding the bargain does not mean refusing every free service. It means making the trade knowingly: checking which permissions an app asks for, switching off location when it is not needed, and asking whether a torch app really needs to see one's contacts.

eng-p026.title: In Defence of the Game
eng-p026.text:
Parents who see a teenager absorbed in a video game for an hour often reach the same verdict: time wasted. I understand the worry, and I share part of it, but I think the verdict is too quick.

Consider what a good strategy game asks of its player. She must hold several goals in mind at once, plan a few moves ahead, notice when a plan is failing and abandon it without sulking. Failure in a game is frequent, public and cheap; the player loses, studies what went wrong and tries again within seconds. Many adults never learn to treat their own mistakes so calmly. Games played with others add another layer: players must divide tasks, communicate under pressure and accept that a teammate's weakness is a problem for the team to solve, not merely to complain about.

None of this means that every game is valuable or that any amount of play is healthy. Some games are built mainly to keep players spending money; others reward nothing but quick reflexes. And an hour stolen from sleep is an hour stolen, whatever the game.

My plea is therefore narrower than it may sound. Before condemning the activity as a whole, parents might sit beside their children for twenty minutes and watch. They may find that what looks like idleness from the doorway is, close up, a kind of practice.

eng-p027.title: No Phones at the Table
eng-p027.text:
In many homes, the evening meal is the one hour when a whole family is in the same room. Increasingly, it is not the same conversation. A father checks cricket scores, a daughter answers a friend, a younger son watches clips with the sound turned low, and the food is eaten in a silence that is not peaceful but merely busy.

I want to propose a rule that sounds old-fashioned: no phones at the table. Not because phones are evil, but because conversation is fragile. It needs pauses, and a pause is precisely the moment when a hand reaches for the screen. A family that is never bored together rarely gets past small talk; the important things, a worry about an exam or a quarrel at work, tend to surface only after the easy topics are exhausted.

Objections come quickly. What if someone calls with something urgent? Then let the phone ring in the next room, where it can be heard. Isn't it unfair to make teenagers obey a rule the adults ignore? Certainly it is, which is why the rule must bind everyone, parents first.

The rule will feel strange for a week. After that, I suspect, many families will find that they had more to say to each other than they knew.

eng-p028.title: How a Feed Learns You
eng-p028.text:
Open a news app or a video site and the list in front of you is not the same list your neighbour sees. It has been arranged for you by a program that studies what you have clicked, how long you stayed and what you skipped. Its aim is simple: to show you more of whatever kept you there last time.

In itself this sounds harmless, even helpful. A reader who loves football is spared stories about fashion. The difficulty appears over months. Each click teaches the program a little more about what pleases you, and each lesson narrows the next list slightly. A reader who once clicked on two angry stories about a rival town may find, a year later, that his feed is full of them. He has not chosen this diet in any deliberate way; it has piled up, one small preference at a time.

Because the narrowing is gradual, it is hard to notice from the inside. The feed feels like a window on the world when it is closer to a mirror, reflecting back the reader's own interests and moods. Some writers call the result a "bubble": a space in which one rarely meets a view one did not already hold.

The program is not malicious; it is doing exactly what it was built to do. The answer lies with readers, who can deliberately follow sources they disagree with and search for news rather than only waiting for it to arrive.

eng-p029.title: The Wrong Fear
eng-p029.text:
Every few years a new machine is said to be coming for our jobs, and every few years the warning is half right. Machines do take over tasks; whole trades have shrunk because of them. Yet the total amount of work has not vanished, because new machines also create needs that did not exist before: someone must install them, repair them, sell them and design what they will do next.

The real danger, I would argue, is not that work will disappear but that the people who lose old jobs will not be the ones who gain the new ones. A middle-aged machine operator in Faisalabad does not become a software designer simply because the economy now needs software designers. The new jobs often appear in different cities, demand different skills and go to the young.

If that is the problem, then the familiar debate, whether to welcome or resist automation, misses the point. Resisting it rarely works for long, and welcoming it without preparation leaves many people stranded. What matters is the bridge between the old work and the new: short, practical courses for adults, help with moving to where the work is, and schools that teach students to keep learning rather than to master one fixed trade.

A machine that does a dull job well is a gift. Whether it feels like a gift to the worker it replaces depends on decisions that people, not machines, will make.

eng-p030.title: Two Ways of Being Known
eng-p030.text:
In a small village, privacy has always been scarce. The shopkeeper knows who bought medicine last week; the neighbours know whose son failed his exams before the result is printed. Many people who move to a city describe the relief of finally being anonymous, of walking down a street where no one knows their name.

The internet seems at first to offer the freedom of the city. Yet in one way it resembles the village more than the city, and in another it is stranger than either. Like the village, it remembers: a photograph or remark can follow a person for years. Unlike the village, it is not watched by people who also know the person's whole story. A neighbour who once saw you lose your temper also saw you help at a funeral; a stranger who finds an old angry post sees only the post.

The village's knowledge, moreover, was mutual. You knew the shopkeeper's affairs as he knew yours, and that balance kept gossip within limits. Online, the watching often runs one way. A company may know a great deal about a user while the user knows almost nothing about who is looking, or why.

Neither arrangement is simply better. But the comparison helps explain why online privacy feels uneasy in a new way: it combines the village's long memory with the city's strangers, and adds an imbalance that neither of them had.

eng-p031.title: From Pulp to Page
eng-p031.text:
Before paper, people wrote on whatever the world offered them. Clay tablets could be pressed with a reed and baked hard, but they were heavy. Animal skins, scraped thin and dried, made a durable surface, yet preparing them was slow and costly. Strips of bark, palm leaves and woven reed sheets served in other places. Each material worked, but none was both cheap and light.

Paper solved this double problem. Its basic method, first developed in China, is surprisingly simple: plant fibres are soaked and beaten until they separate into a soupy pulp, a fine screen is dipped into the mixture, and the thin mat of fibres left on the screen is pressed and dried. The fibres lock together as the water drains away, forming a sheet that is flexible, light and easy to cut. Old rags, hemp and the inner bark of certain trees could all be used, so the raw material was rarely scarce.

The craft travelled slowly, carried along trade routes by merchants and wandering craftsmen. Wherever it arrived, it changed more than writing. Merchants kept fuller accounts, officials issued more orders, and scholars could afford to copy books that had once existed in a single precious version. Paper did not invent learning, but it made learning far less expensive to share, and in that sense its humble pulp carried a quiet revolution.

eng-p032.title: Letters That Stand for Sounds
eng-p032.text:
The earliest writing systems were not designed to record speech at all. They began as tallies and pictures: a small drawing of a sheep beside a row of marks might show how many animals a herder owed. Over time these pictures were simplified and combined, and signs came to stand for whole words or ideas. Such systems were powerful, but they demanded years of training, because a reader had to remember hundreds or even thousands of separate signs.

A crucial shift came when some scribes began to use signs for their sound rather than their meaning. A picture once used for one word could be borrowed to write a different word that merely sounded the same, much as a modern puzzle might use a drawing of an eye to mean the word 'I'. From this habit grew systems in which a small set of signs stood for the basic sounds of a language. An alphabet of a few dozen letters could be learned by a child in months rather than years.

This economy had consequences that reached well beyond the scribe's desk. When reading no longer required a long apprenticeship, it ceased to be the guarded skill of a narrow class of officials and record-keepers. Traders, soldiers and ordinary families could keep accounts and send messages of their own. The alphabet did not make people wiser, but it widened, dramatically, the circle of those who could take part in written life.

eng-p033.title: Telling the Time Without the Sun
eng-p033.text:
For most of history, people did not need to know the time to the minute. The rising and setting of the sun divided the day well enough for farmers, and a shadow cast by a stick or pillar could mark the hours in between. Sundials refined this idea, but they shared its obvious weakness: they were useless at night and on cloudy days.

Other devices tried to free timekeeping from the sky. Water clocks let water drip at a steady rate from one vessel into another, and marks on the side showed how much time had passed. Burning candles and sticks of incense, marked at intervals, did the same job through the slow consumption of wax or powder. Each method worked tolerably, yet each drifted: water flowed faster when the vessel was full, and a draught could make a candle burn unevenly.

Mechanical clocks overcame this by relying on a part that repeats the same small movement again and again, releasing the clock's power in equal steps. Early versions were large, loud and not especially accurate, and many were placed in towers where a whole town could hear them strike. Even so, they began a change in habits. Once a public clock announced the hours, shops opened, workers gathered and meetings started by its signal rather than by the sun. Time, which had been a matter of rough agreement, gradually became something measured, shared and, for better or worse, obeyed.

eng-p034.title: Two Ways of Counting the Year
eng-p034.text:
Every calendar is an attempt to fit human life into the movements of the sky, and the two most familiar approaches start from different lights. A lunar calendar follows the moon. Each month begins with a new crescent and lasts until the next, so anyone who looks up at night can check the date without written tables. This visibility made lunar months natural for herders and travellers, and many communities still use them to fix festivals and other important days.

A solar calendar follows the sun instead, tracking the slow cycle of seasons that decides when rains arrive and crops ripen. For farmers this is the cycle that matters most. The difficulty is that the sun gives no monthly signal; its year must be counted, and errors creep in unless the count is corrected from time to time, which is why solar calendars add an extra day in some years.

The two systems do not fit neatly together. Twelve lunar months fall several days short of a solar year, so a festival fixed by the moon slowly moves through the seasons, arriving in summer in some years and in winter in others. Some societies have accepted this movement; others have added an extra month now and then to pull the moon back in step with the sun. Neither choice is a mistake. Each reflects what a community decided it most needed its calendar to do.

eng-p035.title: Old Maps and New
eng-p035.text:
An old hand-drawn map and the map on a modern phone answer the same question, where am I and how do I get there, but they answer it in very different spirits. The old map was made slowly, from the reports of travellers, merchants and surveyors who walked or sailed the ground. Its maker had to decide what mattered. A well, a river crossing or a friendly town might be drawn large, while empty country was left blank or filled with guesses. Such a map was a kind of argument about which places deserved attention.

A phone map is built from vast collections of measurements and is updated constantly. It rarely leaves anything blank, and it can zoom from a whole country to a single street corner in seconds. Above all, it places a moving dot to show users exactly where they stand. The old map demanded that its reader work out their own position by matching hills and rivers to the drawing; the phone does this work for them.

That convenience has a cost that is easy to miss. A traveller who once had to study the land now often follows instructions without looking up, and may arrive without any picture of the route in their mind. The older map, for all its errors, forced its user to understand the shape of the world. The newer one, for all its precision, can let them pass through that world without noticing it.

eng-p036.title: A Star Over the Water
eng-p036.text:
The screen on Uncle Rashid's boat went dark an hour after sunset, and with it went the little arrow that had guided us all afternoon. I was fifteen, on my first long fishing trip along the Makran coast, and I remember feeling the sea grow suddenly larger. The engine still ran, but the shore had vanished into the dark, and every direction looked the same.

Uncle Rashid did not seem troubled. He switched off the deck light, told me to wait until my eyes adjusted, and pointed upward. 'That one hardly moves,' he said, guiding my gaze to a modest star low in the north. 'Everything else turns around it. Keep it ahead of us, a little to the left, and the coast will come to meet us.' He showed me how the other stars wheeled slowly through the night, and how his own father had judged the hour by their position long before anyone in the village owned a watch.

We reached the harbour a little after midnight. My uncle repaired the screen the next morning and used it for the rest of the trip, without any fuss. But I had noticed something about him that night. He trusted the machine, yet he had never let himself depend on it entirely. I have tried, in other parts of my life, to keep a star in view as well.

eng-p037.title: Paths That Became Roads
eng-p037.text:
Many of the world's roads began as nobody's plan. Animals searching for water wore narrow tracks through grass and scrub, and people followed them because they already led somewhere useful. Over generations, feet and hooves pressed these paths harder, and villages grew where they crossed rivers or met other routes. A road, in this sense, was a record of countless small journeys before it was ever a work of engineering.

Building a road deliberately is a different matter, and the hardest enemy is water. Rain softens bare earth into mud, and cartwheels then cut deep ruts that make the way worse with every passage. The road builders of large ancient states learned to dig down, lay layers of stones of decreasing size, and give the surface a slight curve so that rain would run off into ditches on either side. Such roads could last for centuries, but they were costly, and for long periods only rulers who needed to move armies, officials and taxes could afford them.

Ordinary roads stayed rough far longer than most people imagine. Travellers in many regions put up with dust in summer and mud in the wet months until fairly recent times, when cheaper methods of crushing stone and binding it with tar spread widely. Today we drive across smooth surfaces without a thought, yet beneath them lies the same old lesson: keep the water out, and the road will survive.

eng-p038.title: Why Libraries Still Matter
eng-p038.text:
It is fashionable to say that libraries belong to the past. Almost any fact can be found on a phone, the argument goes, so why keep buildings full of shelves? This view misunderstands what libraries have always been for. From the great collections of the ancient world to the single room above a small town's post office, a library was never only a store of information. It was a promise that knowledge would be available to anyone who walked in, whatever they could afford.

That promise is no less needed today. A student without a quiet room at home, a job seeker without a computer, a retired teacher who cannot buy every new book: these are the people a public library serves, and they have not disappeared. Indeed, as more of life moves online, the gap between those with good access and those without can widen rather than close. A library is one of the few places where that gap is narrowed without anyone being asked to pay or to prove that they deserve help.

None of this means libraries should stand still. The best of them already lend laptops, teach people to judge sources, and host reading circles for children. But such changes are adaptations, not a confession that the idea has failed. A city that closes its library to save money is not merely removing some old books. It is abandoning one of the oldest and fairest bargains a community has ever made with its members.

eng-p039.title: The Power of Nothing
eng-p039.text:
Writing large numbers was once a clumsy business. In many early systems, each value had its own symbol, and a number was shown by repeating symbols and adding them up, much as tally marks are added. Recording a few hundred items was manageable; recording a large sum meant long strings of signs, and doing arithmetic with them was harder still. Merchants often relied on counting boards with pebbles or beads, and wrote down only the answers.

The breakthrough was the idea of place value, which was refined by mathematicians in South Asia and later spread west through Persian and Arab scholars. In this system, a digit's worth depends on where it stands. The same 3 can mean three, thirty or three hundred, depending on how many places lie to its right. Only ten symbols are needed to write any number, however large.

But place value has a hidden requirement: there must be a way to show an empty place. Without one, a reader cannot tell whether a pair of digits means twenty-five or two hundred and five. The answer was a symbol for nothing, a zero, which held a position open. It sounds modest, almost trivial, yet it allowed written sums to be worked out quickly on paper and checked by anyone. Much of later mathematics, from accounting to engineering, depends on this small sign that stands for an absence.

eng-p040.title: Healing Before Laboratories
eng-p040.text:
Long before laboratories and microscopes, healers in every region built up a body of practical knowledge. They watched which plants eased a cough or settled a stomach, and which wounds healed when kept clean and which festered when left dirty. Much of this learning was passed from teacher to student by example, and some of it was written down in collections of remedies that were copied and recopied for generations.

Not all of it was sound. Many early theories explained illness as an imbalance of the body's fluids or elements, and treatments such as bleeding a patient, intended to restore balance, often weakened the sick instead. Because healers could not see the tiny organisms that cause many diseases, they had to rely on guesses about what lay behind the symptoms they could observe.

Yet it would be unfair to dismiss early medicine as mere superstition. Its best practitioners described illnesses carefully, compared cases, and recorded what happened when a treatment was tried. Some of their remedies have been tested by modern researchers and found to contain substances that genuinely work. More importantly, their habit of patient observation laid the groundwork for later methods. The modern doctor who asks how long a fever has lasted and what makes it worse is, in a sense, continuing a conversation that began with those early healers, though now with far better tools for checking the answers.

eng-p041.title: Remembering by Recalling
eng-p041.text:
Most students prepare for a test by reading their notes again and again. The pages begin to look familiar, and that familiarity feels like learning. Unfortunately, it is often an illusion. Recognising a page when it is in front of you is far easier than producing the same ideas from an empty mind, which is exactly what an examination demands.

Teachers who study memory recommend a different habit: closing the book and trying to recall. A student might cover her notes on the causes of a river flood and write down everything she remembers, then check what she missed. The effort of searching for an answer, even when the search partly fails, strengthens the path to that memory. Mistakes made in this kind of private practice are not wasted; they show precisely which parts need more work.

Timing matters as well. Ideas reviewed in one long session the night before a test fade quickly, while the same hours spread over several days tend to last. A short gap allows a little forgetting, and pulling a half-forgotten idea back into the mind seems to fix it more firmly than reviewing something that is still fresh.

None of this makes studying easier. Recalling is slower and more uncomfortable than rereading, and many students abandon it because it feels less productive. That discomfort, however, is a sign that the work is doing its job.

eng-p042.title: The Teenage Body Clock
eng-p042.text:
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and then cannot be woken in the morning. It is easy to call this laziness, but a large part of it is biology. Everyone has an internal clock that tells the body when to feel alert and when to grow drowsy, and during the teenage years this clock shifts later. A fifteen-year-old who lies awake at eleven at night is often not being stubborn; her body simply has not yet sent the signal for sleep.

The trouble is that school does not shift with her. If lessons begin at eight, a student whose body is ready to sleep only around midnight cannot get the long night of sleep that young people need. The shortfall builds up over a week, and its effects are familiar to any teacher: slow thinking in the first period, short tempers, and memories that hold poorly, because much of the work of storing what was learned happens during sleep.

Some habits make the shift worse. Bright screens late in the evening tell the brain that it is still daytime, and long naps after school leave a student wide awake at night. Keeping a fixed time for waking, even on holidays, and putting the phone away an hour before bed will not undo biology, but they can keep a natural delay from turning into a serious lack of sleep.

eng-p043.title: Keep the Games Period
eng-p043.text:
In many schools, the games period is the first thing to disappear when examinations come near. The reasoning sounds sensible: every hour on the field is an hour not spent on physics or mathematics, and marks are what admissions depend on. I believe this reasoning is mistaken, and that cutting sport is a poor bargain even by the narrow measure of results.

A student who sits at a desk from morning until evening does not learn steadily all day. Attention sags, restlessness grows, and the last hours of study often produce very little. Forty minutes of running about does not steal from that study time so much as restore the energy to use it. Pupils who return from the field sweaty and noisy are frequently calmer and sharper an hour later than those who never left their seats.

There is also the matter of what sport teaches. A cricket team that loses heavily on Saturday must still turn up for practice on Monday. Learning to accept a defeat, to rely on others and to keep going when tired is useful preparation for any examination hall, and for a great deal that comes after it.

None of this means that every student must love games or that matches should replace lessons. My point is modest: a school that treats the playground as wasted space is likely to be wasting something far more valuable.

eng-p044.title: Why Pickles Keep
eng-p044.text:
In many Pakistani homes, a jar of mango or lemon pickle sits on the kitchen shelf for months without spoiling, while a bowl of fresh dal left out on a summer afternoon may turn sour by evening. The difference is not luck. Food goes bad mainly because tiny living things, such as bacteria and moulds, settle on it and multiply. Anything that makes life difficult for them helps food to last.

Pickle makers, working long before anyone could see bacteria, discovered several such methods. Salt draws water out of the pieces of fruit, and without water most spoiling organisms cannot grow. Mustard oil poured over the top seals the contents from the air, keeping out new arrivals. Sour ingredients such as lemon juice or vinegar make the mixture too acidic for many of the organisms that would otherwise flourish. Spices add flavour, and some of them may also slow growth a little.

The traditional method, then, is not a single trick but a combination. Each step on its own would protect the food only partly; together they make the jar a very unfriendly place for anything that might rot it. This is also why careless handling can undo the work. A wet spoon dipped into the jar brings water and new organisms with it, and a pickle that has lasted all winter can grow mould within days.

eng-p045.title: Uncle Rafiq's Shop
eng-p045.text:
For thirty years my uncle Rafiq sold nails, paint and padlocks from a narrow shop in the main bazaar of Sabzpur. He kept no computer and needed none; every price was in his head, and every customer was greeted by name. When a large hardware store opened on the new bypass road, with bright lights, wide aisles and a car park, the family assumed his days were numbered.

For a few months they seemed to be. Customers who had bought from Uncle Rafiq for years drove out to the bypass, came back with cheaper paint, and nodded to him a little guiltily as they passed. My cousin Saima, who had just finished her commerce degree, sat with him one evening over the accounts and saw how thin the margins had become.

She did not suggest competing on price; the big store could always undercut them. Instead she looked for what the store could not offer. Its young staff knew where things were kept but not how to fix a leaking tap. Uncle Rafiq knew both. Saima put a small board outside reading "Ask us how", began taking orders over the phone, and arranged for a local plumber to sit in the shop on Saturday mornings.

The shop is busier now than before the store opened. Uncle Rafiq still keeps his prices in his head, but he has, a little grudgingly, allowed Saima to write them in a notebook as well.

eng-p046.title: Choosing a Career
eng-p046.text:
Every year, many students in Pakistan choose between engineering and medicine before they have spent a single day in a hospital or a workshop. The choice is often made by the family, guided by the respect a profession commands and by the success of some cousin who went before. I do not think families should be blamed for wanting security for their children. But I believe that a choice made mainly for prestige is a risky one.

A career lasts forty years or more. Prestige is felt most strongly at a wedding or a family gathering; the work itself is felt every ordinary Tuesday. A student who has no real interest in circuits or in patients may get through a degree on discipline alone, but discipline is harder to sustain over decades than over semesters. Many adults who seem successful on paper describe their working lives as a long endurance.

The remedy is not for young people to defy their parents but to gather evidence before deciding. A week spent shadowing an engineer, a conversation with a junior doctor about night duties, a summer job of any kind: each of these offers something no admission brochure can. Families who encourage such experiments are not giving up their influence; they are making sure it rests on facts.

Interest is not everything. Ability and opportunity matter too. Yet a choice that ignores interest altogether asks a young person to spend a lifetime doing something for other people's reasons.

eng-p047.title: Getting Across Town
eng-p047.text:
In many growing cities, the morning journey to work has become a test of patience. Roads built for a smaller population are now packed with cars, motorcycles and rickshaws, most carrying only one or two people and each taking up road space. Adding lanes seems the obvious answer, yet planners in many countries have found that wider roads often fill up again within a few years, as people who once avoided the rush hour decide to drive after all.

A more lasting solution is to move more people in less space. A single bus can carry as many passengers as dozens of cars, but only if it is quick and reliable enough to tempt drivers out of them. That is the idea behind giving buses their own lanes, separated from the rest of the traffic, with stations where passengers pay before boarding so that loading takes seconds rather than minutes. Where such systems work, the bus stops being the choice of those with no other choice.

Buses alone are not enough, however. A passenger who must walk twenty minutes along a broken pavement in the heat to reach a station will soon give up. Shaded footpaths, safe crossings and cheap rides for the last short distance are dull items in a budget, but they decide whether a fine new bus line is full or half empty.

eng-p048.title: The Message That Never Ends
eng-p048.text:
When Nadia started her small accounting firm, she was proud that clients could reach her team at any hour. A message sent at night was answered by morning, and often within minutes. Within two years, however, she noticed that her staff were tired, that simple tasks took all day, and that mistakes were creeping into accounts that had once been checked with care.

The cause turned out to be the very responsiveness she had been proud of. Each new message pulled someone away from the work in front of them, and returning to a column of figures after an interruption meant finding one's place and one's train of thought all over again. An accountant who was interrupted every ten minutes might spend the whole day busy and still finish nothing that needed real concentration.

Nadia's solution was simple to describe and difficult to keep. Messages would be answered at three fixed times a day, and the hours in between were protected for quiet work. Urgent matters could still be phoned in, but clients were told plainly what counted as urgent. Some grumbled at first. Within a few months, though, the firm was making fewer errors, and several clients remarked that, although replies came more slowly, they now came complete and correct the first time.

She admits that the rule bends during the tax season. It has not yet broken.

eng-p049.title: The Travelling Market
eng-p049.text:
In many Pakistani towns, a market appears once a week on an empty plot or a closed street and vanishes by nightfall. Stalls of vegetables, cloth, plastic buckets and second-hand shoes are set up in the morning, crowded by noon and packed away by evening. To a visitor, it can look chaotic. In fact, the weekly bazaar follows a logic of its own.

Many of its traders are not tied to one place. A vendor may sell in one neighbourhood on Sunday, another on Tuesday and a third on Friday, carrying the same stock from site to site. Because he pays for a pitch only on the days he uses it, his costs are far lower than those of a shopkeeper who must pay rent every month whether customers come or not. Some of that saving reaches the buyer, which is why prices are often lower than in permanent shops.

The arrangement suits customers too. A family that cannot travel far can find, once a week and within walking distance, almost everything a household needs. Because many stalls sell the same goods side by side, buyers can compare quality and price in a few steps, and bargaining is expected rather than rude.

The system has drawbacks. Goods are rarely guaranteed, and a stall that sold faulty sandals last week may not return. Still, for many households, the market's brief, regular life makes it as dependable as any shop.

eng-p050.title: Learning to Make Dal
eng-p050.text:
In my first week at the university hostel, I lived on biscuits, tea and the greasy parathas sold at the gate. At home, food had simply appeared: my mother cooked, and I ate, praised it and occasionally complained that there was too much salt. I had never wondered how a pot of dal became the thick, golden dish that waited for me after school.

In the second week, homesick and slightly ill, I telephoned her and asked for the recipe. She laughed, then grew serious and dictated it slowly while I wrote on the back of a physics worksheet. Soak the lentils. Fry the onions until they are brown, not black. Add the spices to the oil, not to the water. Taste before you add salt. She said this last part twice, and I thought I heard a smile.

My first attempt was a disaster. I was impatient with the onions, the lentils stayed hard, and the smoke alarm in the corridor brought three neighbours to my door. One of them, a quiet final-year student from Swat, showed me that I had used a fierce flame where a gentle one was needed. The second attempt was edible. The fifth, my neighbours agreed, was good.

I still cannot make it taste quite like hers. But every time I stand over that small pot, waiting for the onions to turn, I understand a little better how much patient work was hidden in all those ordinary dinners.

eng-p051.title: The Ledger on the First Day
eng-p051.text:
Hamza reached the office of the Multan Goods Company twenty minutes early, wearing a shirt his mother had ironed twice. He had imagined that his first day as an assistant accountant would involve important meetings. Instead, the senior clerk, a soft-spoken man named Mr. Siddiqui, handed him a dusty ledger and asked him to check three months of delivery receipts against it.

By noon Hamza was bored and a little offended. He had passed his commerce exams with distinction, and here he was ticking columns of figures that a machine could have checked. He worked quickly, eager to finish and be given something worthier of his talents.

In the afternoon, however, he noticed that one transporter's receipts never quite matched the ledger. The gaps were small, a few hundred rupees each time, but they appeared every week. He hesitated, worried that the error might be his own, and then carried the ledger to Mr. Siddiqui's desk.

The old clerk studied the pages for a long time. Then he smiled and admitted that he had suspected the problem for months but had wanted fresh eyes to find it without being told where to look. 'Anyone can add numbers,' he said. 'The job is noticing when they refuse to agree.' Walking home that evening, Hamza realised that the dull task had been a test, and that careful attention, not speed, was the skill being measured.

eng-p052.title: Chalk and Rain
eng-p052.text:
When Rukhsana was posted to the government primary school in Kot Sabir, she found two classrooms, one blackboard and a roof that leaked whenever the clouds gathered. Forty children of different ages shared the space, and many of them came only when their families did not need help in the fields.

Her training college had taught her neat lesson plans, each lasting exactly thirty-five minutes. Within a week she put them aside. The older boys were restless, the youngest girls barely spoke, and the textbooks had arrived missing half their pages. Rukhsana began instead to teach from whatever the village offered. The children measured the length of the courtyard in footsteps, then in metres, and argued about why the answers differed. They wrote letters to relatives in the city, real letters that the postman actually carried away.

Attendance did not rise at once. But slowly the parents noticed that their sons could now check the weight of grain at the market and that their daughters could read the instructions on medicine bottles aloud. One farmer, who had once called the school a waste of good working hours, arrived one morning with a sheet of plastic and nailed it over the worst part of the roof.

Rukhsana never told the district office about the plastic sheet. She suspected it was the most honest report on her work that anyone would ever write.

eng-p053.title: A Night Beside the Rocks
eng-p053.text:
Ayesha had expected the journey north to be a matter of sleeping on the bus and waking up in the mountains. Her grandfather, who had not seen his birthplace in forty years, had other ideas. He kept her awake to look at every river crossing and to repeat the names of villages he half remembered.

On the second day a landslide closed the road ahead. Rocks the size of cars lay across it, and the driver announced that clearing them might take hours or might take until morning. Ayesha sulked. She had a phone with no signal, a bag of biscuits and a grandfather who seemed, irritatingly, delighted by the delay.

Within an hour the stranded passengers had turned the roadside into a small village. A family from Mardan lit a stove and shared their tea. A student going home for the holidays organised a game of cards. Her grandfather told stories about the valley as it had been when the road was only a track, and a crowd gathered to listen.

When the bulldozers finally cleared the way at dawn, Ayesha was almost sorry to leave. Years later, she could hardly remember the village they eventually reached. What stayed with her was that night beside the rocks, when a delay had given strangers a reason to become, briefly, neighbours.

eng-p054.title: The Engine Nobody Could Save
eng-p054.text:
For three weeks the old diesel engine that drove the tube-well at Chak Bahadur had been silent, and the wheat in the nearest fields was beginning to yellow. The landowner sent for a company mechanic from the city, who arrived in a clean van, looked inside for ten minutes and declared that the engine was finished. A new one, he said, would cost more than the season's harvest would earn.

That evening the farmers went to Ustad Karim, who repaired bicycles and radios in a shed behind the market. He was nearly seventy and had never owned a manual. He asked for two days and for a boy to hand him tools. The boy was Imran, the landowner's nephew, who was home from college with nothing to do.

Imran expected to watch an expert work quickly. Instead, Karim worked slowly, laying every part on a clean cloth in the order it came out and listening to the engine whenever he turned it by hand. On the second afternoon he found a cracked fuel pipe hidden behind a bracket, the kind of fault a hurried eye would miss, and shaped a replacement from a length of copper tubing.

When the engine coughed into life, the farmers cheered. Imran, who was studying mechanical engineering, said nothing for a long time. He had learned more about machines in two days of handing over spanners than in a year of lectures.

eng-p055.title: The Borrowed Calculator
eng-p055.text:
In my second year at college I borrowed a calculator from Faraz, a quiet classmate who sat near the window, and I lost it within a week. It was not an expensive model, but it was the only one he had, and our physics practicals were a fortnight away. Instead of telling him, I avoided him. I changed seats, took the long way round the corridor and convinced myself that he had probably forgotten.

He had not. Two days before the practical he asked me, politely, whether he could have it back. I mumbled something about having left it at home. The next day I said the same thing, and the day after that he stopped asking. He did the practical with a borrowed one and never mentioned it again.

At the end of the term I bought him a new calculator, a better one, and I thought that settled the matter. It did not. He thanked me, but there was a small, careful distance in the way he spoke to me afterwards, and it never quite went away.

I have thought about this many times since. The calculator was easy to replace; what I damaged was harder to name. I had not stolen anything, but I had taught a decent person that my word could not be relied upon. These days, when I make a mistake, I try to admit it on the first day, while it is still only a mistake.

eng-p056.title: My Grandmother's Quilts
eng-p056.text:
My grandmother made rillis, the patchwork quilts that families in her part of Sindh spread on beds and give to daughters when they marry. As a child I thought of them simply as blankets, bright and slightly scratchy, piled in a wooden chest that smelled of cloves. It was only when I was twelve, and bored during a long summer, that I sat beside her and asked to learn.

She did not begin with needles. For the first week she made me sort scraps of old clothing by colour and weight, and she talked about where each piece had come from: a cousin's wedding shirt, my grandfather's work kurta, a dupatta that had faded in the sun. I grew impatient and asked when I could start sewing. She laughed and said that a rilli was not made of cloth but of memory, and that I had to know the memory before I could cut it.

My stitches, when I finally made them, were uneven and loose. She unpicked most of them without comment, and I sewed them again. By the end of the summer I had finished one small square, which she worked into the corner of a quilt for my aunt.

I still cannot make a whole rilli. But I understand now that she was teaching me something other than sewing. Each quilt was a family record, and she wanted me to be able to read it.

eng-p057.title: Sadia Runs the Stall
eng-p057.text:
When her father hurt his back lifting a gas cylinder, fifteen-year-old Sadia announced that she would run his tea stall at the bus stand until he recovered. Her mother objected, her uncle laughed, and the regular customers, mostly drivers and conductors, looked doubtful when she appeared behind the counter on the first morning.

The first days were difficult. She burned the milk twice, gave the wrong change to a man in a hurry and ran out of sugar before noon. Yet she noticed things her father had never bothered with. The conductors on the early Sargodha bus had only four minutes, so she began preparing their cups before the bus arrived. An old watchman always asked for less sugar, so she remembered and stopped making him ask.

These small attentions did not go unnoticed. Drivers who had once taken their tea at the larger hotel across the road began to stop at the stall instead. By the end of the month the takings were slightly higher than they had been before the accident.

Her father returned in the sixth week, walking carefully. He looked at the account book, then at the neat row of cups waiting for the Sargodha bus, and said nothing for a while. Then he asked her, rather formally, whether she would be willing to help him on Saturdays. Sadia understood what he could not bring himself to say.

eng-p058.title: Lost in the Old City
eng-p058.text:
Usman was eleven when he let go of his mother's hand in the crowded lanes of the old city and, within a minute, could no longer see her. Every street looked like the last one: the same tangle of wires overhead, the same shops selling bangles and brass, the same motorcycles squeezing past. He walked faster, which only made things worse, and soon he was fighting back tears in a lane he was sure he had never entered.

An elderly man in a tiny bookshop called him in, sat him on a stool and gave him a glass of water. He did not ask many questions. Instead, he asked Usman to describe the last shop he remembered. Usman recalled a green door and a man frying samosas beneath a large clock. The bookseller nodded at once; there was only one such clock in that part of the city.

What surprised Usman most was that the old man did not walk him there. He drew a little map on the back of a receipt, pointed out three turnings and told him to go slowly and read every sign. Usman found the clock in ten minutes, and his frantic mother found him a moment later.

For years he wondered why the bookseller had trusted a frightened boy to find his own way. Only as an adult did he understand the gift: he had been returned not only to his mother but to his own confidence.

eng-p059.title: The Lantern Next Door
eng-p059.text:
The power failed at nine o'clock on the night before Mehwish's chemistry paper, and the whole street went dark. Her phone battery was almost empty, the emergency light had not been charged, and three chapters remained unrevised.
