She sat on the stairs and decided, with the calm of despair, that the exam was lost.

Her younger brother came down from the roof to report that a light was burning on Mrs. Baig's veranda. Mrs. Baig was a retired schoolteacher who lived alone next door and was known on the street mainly for complaining about cricket balls in her garden. Mehwish had spoken to her perhaps twice in her life.

Still, she took her book and knocked. Mrs. Baig, holding an old kerosene lantern, listened, opened the gate and set the lantern on a table between two chairs. Then, instead of leaving her to read, she picked up the textbook and began asking questions. She had taught chemistry for thirty years. When Mehwish confused two reactions, Mrs. Baig drew them side by side on a scrap of newspaper until the difference was obvious.

They worked until the electricity returned after midnight. Mehwish passed the paper comfortably. What she remembered longest, though, was not her result but how wrong she had been about the woman next door, whom the whole street had reduced to a single complaint.

eng-p060.title: The Neem Trees of Station Road
eng-p060.text:
Nobody in Pind Dadan took much notice when Baba Ghulam Nabi began planting neem saplings along the dusty road to the railway station. He was a retired signalman with a bad knee and a bicycle that carried a plastic can of water on each side. Every morning he watered the saplings, and every evening he came back to straighten the ones the goats had pushed over.

People were polite but sceptical. The road was hot and bare, the soil was poor, and the town had seen tree-planting campaigns before. Officials had once come with banners and cameras, planted a hundred trees in an afternoon and never returned. Within a year, most of those trees had died. Why, people asked, would one old man succeed where an entire campaign had failed?

The answer, it turned out, was that he never stopped coming. He planted only a few saplings each season, as many as he could look after himself, and he guarded them like a stubborn parent. When some boys began helping him carry water, he taught them to build little rings of mud around each trunk so that none of it was wasted.

Today the road is shaded for most of its length. The boys are grown men now, and some of them have begun planting trees along the canal. Few of the travellers who rest in that shade know the signalman's name, which, his neighbours say, is exactly how he would have wanted it.

eng-p061.title: The Narrow Window of a Single Exam
eng-p061.text:
Every spring, in towns across Pakistan, students sit in silent halls and, within three hours, turn a year of study into a single number. Parents frame the result, schools print it on banners, and universities sort applicants by it. It is easy to see why: a written exam is cheap to run, the same for everyone, and hard to cheat in when it is well supervised. I do not want to abolish it. I want us to stop pretending that it tells us everything.

A timed paper rewards a particular talent: recalling quickly and writing fast under pressure. Those are useful gifts, but they are not the only ones. The girl who designs a careful experiment over six weeks, or the boy who can explain a hard idea patiently to a struggling classmate, may shine in work that no three-hour paper can capture. When the number is all that counts, such abilities quietly wither, because students sensibly stop spending time on what is never rewarded.

The remedy is not to throw exams away but to place them beside other evidence. A modest share of the final grade could come from projects, marked by teachers and checked by outside moderators so that standards stay fair. Some will object that teachers might favour their own pupils. That risk is real, but it can be managed; the cost of ignoring half of what young people can do is far harder to repair.

eng-p062.title: Less Homework, Better Homework
eng-p062.text:
In many households the evening follows a familiar script. A child arrives home, eats, and then sits down to two or three hours of copying, filling in worksheets and memorising answers for the next day's test. Parents hover, tempers fray, and the work is often finished long after the child has stopped thinking about it. We are told that this is how discipline is built. I am not convinced.

The trouble is not homework itself but its sheer bulk. A short task that asks a pupil to practise a skill learned that morning can fix it in memory far better than any amount of re-reading in class. But a pile of tasks set by six teachers who never compare notes soon becomes a test of stamina rather than understanding. Tired children rush, copy from one another, or let an older sibling do the hard parts, and the teacher who marks the work learns nothing true about what they know.

Schools could fix much of this without spending a rupee. Teachers of the same class might agree on a weekly timetable so that no evening is overloaded, and each task could be designed to take a set number of minutes. Above all, homework should come back with comments, not just ticks. Work that nobody reads teaches children only that effort is pointless, which is the very opposite of discipline.

eng-p063.title: Giving the Old Bazaar Back to Walkers
eng-p063.text:
For decades the old bazaar of Noorpur, a busy town in central Punjab, has been choking. Lanes built for donkey carts and shoppers on foot now carry a stream of cars, motorcycles and delivery vans. Horns compete, fumes hang under the awnings, and a trip that should take ten minutes on foot can take forty by car. Shopkeepers complained that customers were staying away; customers complained that there was nowhere to park.

The town committee's first instinct was to widen the main lane, but that would have meant demolishing shopfronts that had stood for a century. Instead, it tried a cheaper experiment. Cars were barred from the bazaar between ten in the morning and eight at night, a car park was opened on empty land near the bus stand, and small electric rickshaws carried shoppers and their bags the last half-kilometre. Deliveries were allowed only in the early morning.

The first weeks were rough. Some traders feared ruin and protested outside the committee's office. Yet within a few months the number of shoppers had risen, because families who had once avoided the crush began to stroll and linger. This is the lesson other towns should take: a crowded centre is rarely cured by making more room for cars. It is cured by making the centre pleasant for people, and then making it easy for them to arrive.

eng-p064.title: A Valley Can Be Loved to Death
eng-p064.text:
Ten years ago the road into Chinar Dara was a rough track, and the few visitors who reached the valley slept in village guest rooms and ate whatever their hosts had cooked. Today a smooth highway brings thousands every summer weekend. Hotels of raw concrete crowd the riverbank, plastic bottles drift in the streams, and the meadow where shepherds once grazed their flocks has become a car park. The visitors come for the quiet beauty of the mountains, and in coming they are destroying it.

Some argue that tourism is the valley's only hope. It brings money to a place that had little, they say, and no one has the right to tell poor villagers to stay poor so that city people can enjoy an empty view. That argument deserves respect. But much of the money does not stay in the valley at all. It flows to hotel owners and tour companies from the cities, while the villagers are left with the litter, the noise and rising prices.

The answer is not to close the valley but to manage it. A daily limit on vehicles, a modest entry fee spent on collecting waste, and rules that keep new buildings away from the river would cost visitors little. Licences for guides and guest houses could be kept for local families, so that those who live with the crowds also share in the earnings. A valley that is visited wisely can welcome people for generations; one that is merely exploited will soon have nothing left to offer.

eng-p065.title: Page and Screen
eng-p065.text:
Ask a group of students whether they prefer to read on paper or on a screen, and the answers will divide sharply. Screens have obvious advantages. A single phone can hold a library, a puzzling word can be looked up with one tap, and a text can be enlarged for tired eyes or searched in seconds for a half-remembered phrase. For a student in a small town far from a good bookshop, that access is no small thing.

Paper, however, has strengths that are easier to overlook. A printed book has a shape: you can feel how far you have come and how much remains, and you often remember that a key argument sat near the bottom of a left-hand page. Many readers say that this sense of place helps them recall what they have read. A book also does only one thing. It does not buzz with messages or tempt you to check the cricket score, so your attention is less likely to be broken.

Neither medium, then, is simply better. Screens suit quick searching, short articles and texts we need to carry everywhere; paper suits long, demanding reading that must be understood and remembered. The sensible reader does not take sides in a contest between them but chooses the tool that fits the task, perhaps skimming the news on a phone while keeping the chemistry textbook open on the desk.

eng-p066.title: Racing Ahead or Pulling Together
eng-p066.text:
Walk into two schools in the same city and you may find two different philosophies. In the first, rankings are posted on the noticeboard every month, prizes go to the top three in each class, and pupils know exactly where they stand against their friends. In the second, children work in small groups, share marks for joint projects, and are praised for helping a slower classmate as much as for their own scores.

Each approach has its defenders, and each has a point. Competition can spur effort: a pupil who sees a rival's name above her own may study harder than any lecture could make her. But it can also turn learning into a contest in which one child's success seems to require another's failure, and those near the bottom of the list may simply give up. Cooperation builds the patience and teamwork that most adult jobs demand, yet in a careless group the strongest member may do all the work while the others drift along on borrowed credit.

The wisest schools seem to borrow from both. They let pupils test themselves against a fixed standard, or against their own last result, rather than against each other, and they design group tasks in which every member has a part that can be seen and checked. In this way the energy of competition and the generosity of cooperation can work together instead of pulling apart.

eng-p067.title: Keep the Small-Town Library Open
eng-p067.text:
When councillors in the small town of Mianpur proposed closing its public library last year, their reasoning sounded sensible. Fewer people were borrowing books, almost everyone had a phone, and the building's roof needed costly repairs. Why spend scarce money on shelves of old novels when the internet offers more than any library could hold?

The argument is tidy, and it is wrong. A library has never been only a store of books. In Mianpur it is the one quiet, well-lit room where a student whose family of five shares two rooms can study after dark. It is where a retired clerk reads the newspapers he can no longer afford, and where a librarian who knows her readers can put the right book into a hesitant teenager's hands. A phone offers information; it does not offer a desk, a silence or a guide.

Nor is falling borrowing a sign that the need has gone. It may simply show that the library has been neglected: its hours cut, its stock never renewed, its existence barely advertised. Before a town abandons such a place, it should at least try reviving it by opening in the evenings, adding a few computers and inviting schools to visit. A library that is lost is seldom rebuilt, and those who suffer most from its absence are the ones least able to complain.

eng-p068.title: In Praise of Repair
eng-p068.text:
My grandfather owned one radio for thirty years. When it fell silent, he carried it to a man in the bazaar who opened it on a cluttered bench, replaced a part no bigger than a grain of rice, and handed it back the same afternoon. Today, when a phone or a blender stops working, most of us do not even ask whether it can be fixed. We throw it away and buy another.

This habit is often defended as progress. New machines are cheaper, faster and more efficient, the argument goes, and repair is for people who cannot afford anything better. But the low price on the shop shelf hides costs that someone else pays: the mines that dig out the metals, the factories that burn fuel, and the heaps of discarded electronics that leak poisons into the soil. A gadget that lasts three years instead of ten simply multiplies these costs.

Repair also keeps alive a kind of knowledge that our schools rarely teach: the patient, practical understanding of how things actually work. The repairers in our bazaars are skilled people, and their trade is dwindling. We could support them by choosing products that can be opened and mended, and by asking makers to sell spare parts. Fixing a thing is not a sign of poverty. It is a small act of good sense, and of respect for the effort that went into making it.

eng-p069.title: A Skill in the Hands
eng-p069.text:
In many Pakistani families, a child who does well at school is steered towards medicine or engineering, while one who does not is told, kindly or otherwise, that a trade is the fallback. Electricians, tailors, welders and mechanics are needed in every street, yet their work is spoken of as something one settles for, not something one chooses.

This attitude is costly. A skilled electrician who wires houses safely protects lives as surely as many office workers who earn far more respect. Demand for good tradespeople is steady, both at home and abroad, and a capable plumber with a name for honesty may earn more than a graduate stuck in a poorly paid clerical post. Meanwhile, young people who would thrive working with their hands are pushed into degrees they neither want nor finish, and they leave with debts and a sense of failure.

Changing this will take more than speeches. Technical colleges need modern equipment and teachers who have actually worked in their trades, and employers need to pay for skill rather than for certificates alone. Most of all, parents and teachers need to stop using the word "only", as in "only a mechanic" or "only a tailor". A society that respects the people who build and mend its world will find that more of its brightest young people are willing to join them.

eng-p070.title: Record the Old Voices
eng-p070.text:
Every family has someone who remembers. It may be a grandmother who can describe the village before the canal came, or an uncle who recalls how a wedding was arranged sixty years ago, who sang which songs and what was cooked. Such memories are rarely written down. They live in conversation, and when the person who holds them dies, they usually vanish too.

Historians have long relied on official papers: government records, newspapers and the letters of the educated few. These sources are valuable, but they tell us mostly about people who held power or who wrote for a living. The farmer, the potter and the woman who ran a household of twelve left few documents behind. If we want to know how ordinary lives were actually lived, we must listen to the people who lived them while we still can.

The task is not difficult, and that is precisely why it is so often neglected. A phone can record an hour of talk; a student can ask a grandparent a few patient questions on a winter evening. Schools could make such interviews a holiday project, and local colleges could gather them into simple archives. Some will say that these recollections are unreliable, coloured by age and affection. They are, but so are many official records, and a memory that is imperfect is still worth more than one that is lost.

eng-p071.title: Weighing the Air
eng-p071.text:
For most of history, air seemed to be nothing at all. Many scholars taught that nature hates an empty space and rushes to fill any gap, and this idea seemed to explain why water rises up a drinking straw. Pump-makers, however, had noticed an awkward fact: no matter how hard they worked, a suction pump could not lift water more than about ten metres.

In the seventeenth century, a few experimenters began to suspect that this limit was a clue. Perhaps water was not pulled up by the emptiness above it but pushed up by the weight of the air pressing on the open water below. To test the idea, they filled a long glass tube with mercury, a liquid far heavier than water, and turned it upside down in a bowl of the same liquid. The mercury sank a little and then stopped, leaving a gap at the top of the tube. The column that remained was much shorter than ten metres, just as the idea predicted, since a heavier liquid needs less height to balance the same weight of air.

The experiment did more than settle an argument. Observers soon noticed that the column rose and fell slightly from day to day, and that it stood lower on a mountain than in a valley. The tube had become an instrument for measuring the air itself. The lesson behind it has never gone out of date: an inconvenient fact, carefully followed, can overturn an idea that everyone accepts.

eng-p072.title: The Covered Jar
eng-p072.text:
For centuries, many careful observers believed that some living things could arise from lifeless matter. Leave meat in the open for a few days, and maggots appear in it; store grain in a damp corner, and mice seem to emerge from the sacks. To people who had no way of watching every fly that landed or every mouse that crept in, the conclusion seemed obvious: rotting meat produced worms, and old grain produced mice.

The idea was eventually challenged not by argument but by a simple arrangement of jars. An experimenter placed pieces of meat in several jars. Some he left open; others he sealed tightly. Before long, maggots crawled in the open jars, while the meat in the sealed jars rotted without a single worm. Critics objected that sealing the jars had shut out the fresh air that life required. So he repeated the test, this time covering some jars with fine cloth, which let air in but kept flies out. Flies gathered on the cloth and even laid eggs on it, but the meat beneath stayed free of maggots.

The beauty of the experiment lay in its comparison. Every jar was treated alike except in one respect, so any difference in the result could be traced to that single change. This way of thinking, now called a controlled experiment, sounds simple, yet it remains one of the most powerful tools science has. It does not depend on clever instruments, only on the discipline to change one thing at a time.

eng-p073.title: Shells on the Hill
eng-p073.text:
On a school trip to the Salt Range, Bilal picked up a grey stone from the path and nearly threw it away before he saw the pattern on it: the fine, fan-shaped ridges of a seashell, pressed into the rock. He held it up to Miss Kausar, their geography teacher, and asked the obvious question. How could a shell end up on a hill hundreds of kilometres from the sea?

Miss Kausar did not answer at once. Instead she told the class that people had been asking the same question for a very long time. Some early thinkers decided that such stones had grown inside the rock by themselves and only happened to look like shells. Others claimed that a great flood had once carried sea creatures over the mountains. A few, looking more closely, noticed that the shells lay in flat layers, one above another, like pages in a book, which is not how a sudden flood leaves things. They reached a bolder conclusion: the rock had once been the floor of a sea, and the land itself had slowly risen.

"That idea seemed absurd to most people," she said, "because nobody had ever seen a mountain move." She explained that the rise was far too slow to watch in a lifetime, and that only patient study of the rocks had made it believable. Bilal turned the stone over in his palm. Ten minutes earlier it had been rubbish under his shoe. Now it felt like a message that had waited a very long time to be read.

eng-p074.title: Wrong in a Useful Way
eng-p074.text:
We tend to remember the history of science as a parade of correct ideas, each one a step closer to the truth. The wrong ideas are quietly dropped from the story, as if they had been nothing but obstacles. This is a mistake, because a good wrong theory can do as much to move knowledge forward as a right one.

Consider an old explanation of burning. Many chemists once held that anything that could burn contained a hidden substance which escaped into the air as flames. Wood left only a little ash because most of its burning substance had gone. The theory was tidy, and it explained a great deal. But it also made a prediction that could be checked: a metal heated until it crumbled into a powder should, having lost something, weigh less. When careful workers weighed the powder, they found the opposite. It weighed more.

That surprising result did not come from ignoring the old theory but from taking it seriously enough to test. It pointed researchers towards the idea that burning involves taking something from the air, not giving something to it, and so opened the way to a new understanding of chemistry. Students who memorise only the final answer miss this lesson. Being wrong is not the failure in science; refusing to find out whether you are wrong is.

eng-p075.title: Circles or Signals?
eng-p075.text:
At a busy crossing, traffic engineers usually choose between two tools: a set of traffic lights or a roundabout. Each deals with the same problem, cars arriving from several directions and wanting the same piece of road, but each does it in a very different way.

Traffic lights work by taking turns. For a fixed period one stream moves while the others wait, and then the right of way passes on. This makes signals predictable and easy to understand, and they suit crossings where pedestrians need a protected moment to cross. Their weakness is waste. At night, or when one road is quiet, drivers may sit at a red light facing an empty junction, burning fuel and patience.

A roundabout, by contrast, asks drivers to judge gaps for themselves. Cars entering give way to those already circling and slip in when there is space, so no one waits for a light to change. Because every vehicle must slow down and turn, the violent head-on and side impacts that make some crossings deadly become rare; collisions that do occur tend to be glancing ones. Yet roundabouts have limits too. When traffic from one direction is very heavy, drivers on the other roads may wait a long time for a gap, and a large roundabout can be hard for people on foot.

Neither tool, then, is simply better. The right choice depends on how much traffic arrives, from where, and who else needs to use the space.

eng-p076.title: Steel on Steel
eng-p076.text:
A loaded goods train can weigh thousands of tonnes, yet a single locomotive can pull it along a level track. The secret lies not so much in the engine's power as in the meeting of two hard surfaces: a steel wheel rolling on a steel rail.

When a rubber tyre rolls along a road, it flattens slightly where it touches the ground and springs back as it turns. That constant squashing and recovering uses up energy, which is one reason a lorry needs a large engine and plenty of fuel. A steel wheel barely changes shape at all. The patch where it meets the rail is tiny, no larger than a coin, and very little energy is lost in rolling. As a result, moving goods by rail can take far less fuel for each tonne than moving them by road.

The same hardness, however, brings a drawback. Because steel slides over steel so easily, a train has little grip. It cannot climb steep slopes, which is why railway lines curve around hills or pass through tunnels where a road would simply go over the top. It also needs a long distance to stop, so signals must warn drivers well in advance. Engineers have learned to work with this trade-off rather than against it. They lay tracks along gentle gradients and plan stopping distances with care, accepting slower, longer routes in exchange for the remarkable efficiency of steel on steel.

eng-p077.title: The Night Bus to Multan
eng-p077.text:
I had expected to sleep through the night bus from Lahore to Multan, but the seat beside the driver was the only one left, and sleep never came. The driver, a broad, quiet man called Akram, kept a flask of tea wedged beside the gear lever and a small towel over one shoulder. For the first hour he said almost nothing, and I assumed he resented having a passenger so close to his elbow.

Somewhere past Okara, a truck without tail-lights loomed out of the dark, and Akram eased around it so smoothly that most of the passengers never woke. Only then did he begin to talk. He had driven this road for nineteen years, he said, and he knew it the way some people know a song: where the surface broke up after the rains, which villages sent cattle across at dawn, where tired drivers tended to drift. He did not trust the bright new road signs. "They tell you what the road should be," he said, "not what it is tonight."

By the time the sky paled over the cotton fields, I had stopped thinking of the journey as dead time between two cities. Forty people had slept safely because one man stayed awake and paid attention. When we pulled into Multan, the passengers stretched, collected their bags and hurried off. Hardly anyone looked back at the driver. I did, and he raised his tea flask to me, as if we had shared a secret.

eng-p078.title: Free Parking Is Never Free
eng-p078.text:
In most of our cities, parking a car on the street costs nothing, and many drivers would regard a charge as an outrage. Yet free parking is a curious kind of gift. The land under a parked car is valuable; it could hold a wider footpath, a fruit seller's cart, a bus stop or a row of trees. When the space is given away, someone still pays for it, only not the driver.

Consider a busy market street where every space is free. Drivers arrive, find the kerb full, and circle slowly looking for a gap, adding to the very congestion that annoys them. Shopkeepers complain that customers cannot stop, yet the spaces outside their doors are often filled all day by a few early arrivals, sometimes the shopkeepers themselves. The street is crowded not because there are too few spaces but because the spaces are priced at zero.

A modest charge, rising at the busiest hours, would change behaviour without banning anyone. Long-stay parkers would move to cheaper places a short walk away, leaving room for quick visits, and drivers would stop circling because a space would usually be free. The money could repair the pavements that pedestrians have long been denied. None of this is a war on motorists. It is simply a matter of asking those who use valuable public land to pay a fair share of its value, as we expect of anyone else.

eng-p079.title: The Ache That Comes Later
eng-p079.text:
Anyone who has returned to exercise after a long break knows the pattern. The workout itself feels manageable, and the evening passes without complaint. Then, a day or two later, climbing stairs becomes an ordeal and sitting down is a careful, groaning business. The soreness has arrived late, and for a long time many people blamed it on acid left behind in the muscles.

That explanation does not fit the timing. The acid produced during hard effort is cleared from the blood within an hour or so, long before the ache begins. Many researchers now believe the soreness comes instead from tiny tears in muscle fibres, together with the body's response to them. The damage is greatest in movements where a muscle lengthens while it works, such as lowering a heavy load or walking down a steep hill. Repairing these small injuries takes time, and the swelling and tenderness that come with the repair are what we feel.

This sounds alarming, but it is mostly a sign of adaptation. Muscles that recover from such tears become better able to resist them, which is why the second session of a new exercise usually hurts far less than the first. The practical lesson is not to avoid effort but to increase it gradually. A beginner who attempts a long downhill run on the first day is inviting a painful week; one who builds up over a fortnight may barely notice the change.

eng-p080.title: The Coach Who Said Less
eng-p080.text:
When I joined the under-sixteen team at our club in Sialkot, I expected the coach to shout. Every coach I had known shouted. But Master Yousaf, a thin man with a cracked bat he never seemed to use, hardly spoke at all. On my first evening he watched me bowl twenty balls, nodded, and walked away. I went home convinced that he had already written me off.

The next week he placed a single plastic cup on the pitch, a little short of a good length, and told me to hit it. Nothing else. I bowled and bowled. Most balls sprayed down the leg side; a few went near the cup. After half an hour, without any help from him, I noticed that the good ones came when I kept my head still at the moment of release. When I told him, he smiled for the first time. "Good," he said. "Now you know it. If I had told you, you would only have heard it."

I have had louder coaches since then, men full of advice and diagrams. I learned things from them, too. But the lessons that stayed with me were the ones Master Yousaf let me find for myself, with a cup, a ball and his patient silence. Years later, coaching boys of my own, I catch myself wanting to explain everything at once, and I remember that cup, and I keep quiet a little longer.

eng-p081.title: The Training Happens at Rest
eng-p081.text:
Ask a keen young athlete how to get fitter and the answer is almost always the same: train more. Run further, lift heavier, practise longer. Rest days are treated as a weakness, something to apologise for, and the athlete who trains every day without a break is admired as the most dedicated in the squad.

This attitude misunderstands how the body improves. Hard training does not make a person stronger on the day it is done; if anything, it leaves muscles tired and slightly damaged, and performance the next morning is often worse. The improvement comes afterwards, during recovery, when the body repairs itself and builds up a little more capacity than before, as if preparing for the next demand. Training is the signal; rest is when the answer is built. Cut out the rest and the signal keeps arriving with no time for a reply.

The results of ignoring this are familiar to any coach: nagging injuries, heavy legs, falling times and, often, a loss of joy in the sport. None of this means that rest days should be lazy days spent in front of a screen. Gentle movement, good sleep and proper meals are part of the work. But athletes, and the people who train them, need to stop treating recovery as time lost. It is the half of training that nobody sees, and it is no less important for being quiet.

eng-p082.title: Playing Alone, Playing Together
eng-p082.text:
Parents choosing a sport for a child often ask which is better: a team game such as hockey or football, or an individual sport such as badminton, swimming or athletics. The honest answer is that they teach different lessons, and a child may need one more than the other.

A team game is a lesson in belonging. A footballer who scores has usually been helped by three or four others, and one who makes a mistake is covered by a teammate. Children learn to share credit, to accept a role that may not be glamorous, and to keep trying for others when they would happily give up for themselves. The disadvantage is that a quiet child can hide in a team, touching the ball rarely and never quite discovering what he or she can do.

An individual sport offers no such hiding place. The swimmer who finishes last cannot blame a defender, and the badminton player who wins knows that the victory is entirely her own. This builds a clear sense of responsibility and a habit of honest self-assessment. It can also be lonely and, for an anxious child, harsh, since every failure is personal.

Wise parents therefore look less at the sport and more at the child. A shy child might flourish when carried along by a team; a child who leans too heavily on others might grow by standing alone for a while.

eng-p083.title: Why a Flat Field Saves Water
eng-p083.text:
To the eye, most fields look flat. To water, they are not. When a farmer opens a channel and lets water flow across a field that is a few centimetres higher at one end, the water races to the low corners and lies there in pools, while the high patches stay dry. To wet those patches, the farmer must keep the water running far longer than the crop needs, and much of it soaks uselessly below the roots or drowns the plants in the hollows.

Levelling the field solves this. In the past it was done by eye, with a wooden board dragged behind oxen, and the results were rough. Today many farmers hire a tractor whose scraper is guided by a laser beam sent from a stand at the edge of the field. The beam marks a perfectly level plane, and the scraper rises and falls automatically, shaving soil from the high spots and leaving it in the low ones.

The benefits go beyond water. When the whole field is wetted evenly, seeds sprout at the same time and the crop ripens together, which makes harvesting easier. Fertiliser is less likely to be washed into the hollows. The main obstacle is cost: few small farmers can buy such equipment, and so the service usually spreads where a contractor, a cooperative or a local scheme makes it possible to rent a tractor for a day.

eng-p084.title: At the Tail of the Watercourse
eng-p084.text:
My father's land lies at the very end of a long watercourse, the last fields before the channel runs out into a dry ditch. Every farmer along it has a fixed turn to take water, measured in hours and minutes, and ours came on Thursday nights. As a boy I thought this was a fair system. Each family had its turn; what could be fairer?

It took me years to understand my father's worry on those nights. By the time the water reached us, it had passed thirty farms. Some of it had soaked into the earth banks along the way, and some had been quietly taken by neighbours who left their outlets open a little too long. Our turn lasted as many hours as anyone's, but the stream that arrived was thin and tired. I remember him walking the channel with a lantern, pressing mud into small breaks in the bank, never shouting at anyone, simply trying to save what he could.

Last year the farmers along the watercourse agreed to line it with bricks, sharing the cost, and to check each other's outlets. I was home when the water came on the first Thursday after the work was finished. It reached our fields quickly, fast and clear. My father stood at the edge of the channel for a long time, not saying anything. Then he went to bed early, for the first Thursday night that I could remember.

eng-p085.title: Keeping the Old Seeds
eng-p085.text:
In many villages, the seed a farmer sows today comes from a shop, not from last year's harvest. The new varieties sold there often give heavier yields, and few farmers would want to give them up. But something has been lost in the change. Older local varieties, each saved and resown by families over generations, are disappearing, and with them go traits that nobody may think to value until they are needed: a wheat that survives a late frost, a millet that ripens on very little rain, a pulse that pests seem to ignore.

Once a variety is gone, it cannot be bought back. That is why some communities have begun keeping seed banks of their own. These are not grand buildings but simple rooms with clay pots or sealed tins, each labelled with the name of the variety and the family that grew it. A farmer may borrow a few kilograms at sowing time and return a larger amount after the harvest, so the stock is renewed instead of slowly ageing on a shelf.

Such banks will not feed a country on their own, and they are no argument against modern seed. Their value is quieter: they keep choices open. In a run of good years, the old varieties may seem a sentimental hobby; in a year of drought or a new disease, a pot of forgotten seed in a village room might be worth more than any shop's stock.

eng-p086.title: Renting the Bees
eng-p086.text:
In spring, a strange cargo travels along the roads of some fruit-growing valleys: wooden boxes, stacked on the backs of pick-up trucks, each humming with thousands of bees. Their owners are not delivering honey. They are renting out their bees to orchard owners for a few weeks while the trees are in flower.

The reason lies in how fruit forms. An apricot or apple blossom cannot become fruit until pollen, the fine dust made by the flower, has been carried from one blossom to another, often from a different tree. Wind does little of this work for such trees. Insects do most of it, brushing against the pollen as they gather nectar and leaving some on the next flower they visit. Where wild insects are plentiful, an orchard may need no help. But large orchards, with acres of a single crop and few hedges or wild flowers nearby, often have too few wild insects to visit every blossom in the short time the trees are in flower.

Hired hives fill this gap. Growers who use them often report heavier, more even crops, and the beekeepers earn a fee as well as the honey their bees collect. The arrangement has one condition that both sides must respect. If the orchard is sprayed with insect poison while the trees are in bloom, the visitors will die along with the pests. A good agreement therefore says as much about when not to spray as about how many hives to bring.

eng-p087.title: Centring the Clay
eng-p087.text:
Watch a skilled potter at the wheel and the first minute looks like nothing at all. A lump of wet clay is slapped onto the spinning disc, and the potter leans over it, hands cupped, pressing and easing, pressing and easing. No pot appears. Yet this stage, called centring, decides whether everything that follows will succeed.

A lump that is even slightly off-centre wobbles as it turns. Each time the high side passes the potter's fingers, it is pushed harder than the low side, so the wobble grows rather than shrinks. If the potter tries to open the lump and raise its walls at this point, one side of the pot will be thicker than the other. The thin side may collapse while the pot is still on the wheel, or crack later in the kiln as the uneven walls dry and shrink at different rates.

Centring corrects this by forcing the clay to run true. The potter braces the elbows against the body or the knees, so that the hands become a fixed guide rather than following the clay's movement, and lets the spinning wheel do the work. Beginners usually fight the clay, gripping hard and chasing the wobble. Experienced potters do the opposite: they hold still and steady and let the clay come to them. It is a lesson that apprentices often say applies well beyond the wheel.

eng-p088.title: The First Clean Print
eng-p088.text:
My aunt has printed cloth in her courtyard in Hala for as long as I can remember, and the summer I turned sixteen she finally let me hold a block. It was carved from heavy wood, its face cut into a pattern of tiny leaves, and it smelled of dye and old oil. "Press once," she said. "Don't rock it. Don't lift it to look."

I rocked it, of course, and I lifted it to look. My first prints came out blurred at one edge and pale at the other. When I tried to fix a pale patch by pressing again, I doubled the outline and spoiled the whole length of cloth. My aunt said nothing. She simply laid out another strip and handed the block back. By the end of the week I had ruined more cotton than I liked to count, and I was sure she regretted the waste.

Then, one morning, I stopped thinking about the block and watched her hands instead: the way she loaded it evenly from the dye pad, set it down with her wrist straight and struck the back once with the heel of her palm. I copied the movement exactly. When I lifted the block, the leaves sat on the cloth, sharp and dark and whole. I looked up, expecting praise. She only nodded and said, "Now do it four hundred more times." I laughed, but I understood. One good print was luck; a whole cloth of them would be skill.

eng-p089.title: Reading the Grain
eng-p089.text:
Ask a carpenter why a chair leg snapped, and the first thing he will look at is not the joint or the glue but the grain. Wood is made of long fibres that run along the length of the trunk like bundles of drinking straws. Along those fibres, wood is remarkably strong; a thin strip is hard to snap. Yet the fibres are held to one another only weakly, so a blow in line with the grain can split a log in two, which is exactly how firewood is cut.

A good carpenter therefore cuts each part so that its grain follows the direction of the load it must carry. A chair leg is sawn from a piece in which the fibres run from top to bottom; if the grain crosses the leg at a slant, the fibres are short and the leg may break where the slant meets the surface.

Grain matters for another reason. Fresh wood is full of water, and as it dries it shrinks, but not evenly: far more across the grain than along it. A table top made from damp planks may look perfect in the workshop and open wide cracks a few months later in a dry room. This is why careful workshops stack new timber with gaps between the boards and leave it, sometimes for a year or more, before they cut it. Impatience is costly in this trade; the wood will always have the last word.

eng-p090.title: A Fair Price for the Weaver
eng-p090.text:
In a weaving village, a shawl can take a woman three weeks at the loom. When she sells it, she usually sells it to the same trader who supplied the yarn, often on credit, and the price is whatever he names. In a city shop the same shawl may sell for several times as much. The difference does not vanish; it is shared among the trader, the wholesaler and the shopkeeper, each of whom does some real work. But the woman who made the thing is left with the smallest share and the least say.

It is tempting to blame the trader, but he is a symptom more than a cause. The weaver depends on him because she has no other way to buy yarn in bulk, no means of reaching distant buyers and no savings to wait for a better offer. Take away the trader without replacing what he provides, and she would be worse off.

The more useful answer has been for weavers to act together. Where a group of them has formed a cooperative, it can buy yarn at wholesale prices, hold stock until a fair offer comes, and sell directly to shops or through exhibitions. Such groups need patience, honest bookkeeping and someone who can deal with buyers, and many fail. Yet the ones that last show what is possible: not charity, but craftswomen who are finally paid something close to what their work is worth.

eng-p091.title: How Birds Find Their Way
eng-p091.text:
Each autumn, small birds that weigh less than a coin leave the cold north and fly thousands of kilometres to warmer lands, many of them passing over Pakistan on the way. Some return in spring to the very same hedge they left. For a long time this feat baffled observers, who could not see how a creature with a brain the size of a pea could navigate so precisely.

The answer, scientists now believe, is that birds do not rely on a single guide but carry several. By day, many steer by the sun, allowing for its movement across the sky with an inner sense of time. On clear nights, young birds learn the pattern of stars that turns around the pole and use it as a fixed point. When clouds hide both, a sense of the earth's magnetism seems to tell them which way is north. Close to home, familiar rivers, coastlines and even smells take over.

This redundancy is what makes the system so dependable. A pilot with only one instrument is in trouble the moment it fails; a pilot with four can afford to lose one. In the same way, a bird blown off course by a storm, or flying under an overcast sky, simply leans more heavily on whichever cues remain.

The arrangement is not flawless. Bright city lights can confuse night travellers, and each year some birds end up far from where they meant to go. But for the great majority, the journey ends where it should.

eng-p092.title: The Silent Flight of the Owl
eng-p092.text:
Most birds are noisy fliers. A pigeon taking off from a rooftop claps its wings loudly, and even a small sparrow makes a soft whirr as it passes. An owl hunting at dusk, by contrast, can glide within a metre of a mouse without being heard. This silence is not luck; it is the product of feathers shaped in three unusual ways.

First, the leading edge of each main wing feather carries a row of stiff, comb-like fringes. Instead of slicing the air in one sharp line, the wing breaks it into many small streams, which mix more quietly. Second, the trailing edge is soft and ragged, so that air leaving the wing does not snap off in a single noisy wave. Third, the upper surface of the feathers is covered in a velvety down that muffles the rub of feather against feather as the wing beats.

These features cost the owl something. Its soft feathers soak up rain easily, which is one reason owls rarely hunt in heavy downpours, and they do not allow the bursts of speed that a falcon achieves. The owl has, in effect, traded speed and weatherproofing for stealth.

Engineers have taken note. Some designers of fans and wind turbines have begun adding serrated edges to their blades, hoping to borrow a little of the owl's quiet. The bird, after all, has had a very long time to perfect its design.

eng-p093.title: Why Lakes Freeze from the Top
eng-p093.text:
In the high valleys of Gilgit-Baltistan, winter can freeze lakes hard enough to walk on. Yet beneath the ice, fish survive until spring. They owe their lives to an odd habit of water that sets it apart from almost every other liquid.

Most substances shrink as they cool and become densest when solid; a block of solid wax sinks in a pot of melted wax. Water behaves this way only down to about four degrees Celsius. Below that point it begins to expand slightly, and when it finally freezes, the ice is lighter than the water around it. As a lake cools in autumn, the colder surface water sinks and warmer water rises to take its place, until the whole lake has reached about four degrees. After that, the surface water cools further but, being lighter, stays on top. It freezes there, forming a lid.

That lid matters enormously. Ice is a poor conductor of heat, so it acts like a blanket, slowing the loss of warmth from the water below. The deeper water stays liquid, at a steady temperature that is cold but bearable for fish.

Imagine water behaving like wax. Ice would form at the surface, sink, and pile up on the lakebed, layer after layer, until in a hard winter the lake froze solid from the bottom upward. Little in it could survive. A small quirk of one substance, in other words, makes winter life in cold lakes possible.

eng-p094.title: Why Sunsets Turn Red
eng-p094.text:
At noon on a clear day the sky over the Thar is a deep, even blue. By evening the same sky may blaze orange and red around the setting sun. The air has not changed colour; what has changed is the length of the path that sunlight takes through it.

Sunlight looks white but is a mixture of all colours. As it passes through the atmosphere, it strikes countless tiny particles of gas, and these scatter some of the light sideways in every direction. Crucially, they do not treat all colours alike: blue light, with its shorter waves, is scattered far more strongly than red. At midday, when the sun is high and its light crosses a fairly thin layer of air, enough blue is scattered across the sky to tint it from horizon to horizon, while the sun itself still looks almost white.

At sunset the geometry is different. The sun sits low, and its light must slant through a much thicker slice of atmosphere before it reaches us. Along that long route, most of the blue is scattered away long before it arrives, leaving the reds and oranges, which pass through more easily. Dust and smoke in the air can deepen the effect, which is why some of the most vivid sunsets follow a dry, windy day.

The same rule explains why distant mountains often look bluish. Between the viewer and the slopes lies a great deal of air, and it adds its own faint blue glow.

eng-p095.title: Building for the Shaking
eng-p095.text:
When an earthquake strikes, it is rarely the shaking itself that kills people; it is the buildings that fall on them. In many mountain villages, houses are made of heavy stones stacked with weak mud mortar and topped with a thick, flat roof. Such a house stands perfectly well for decades, because ordinary life presses on it only from above. A strong quake, however, pushes it sideways, back and forth, and the loose walls simply peel apart, bringing the heavy roof down.

The obvious answer, building every home from reinforced concrete, is out of reach for most families, and concrete poorly made can be deadlier than stone. Engineers working in such areas have therefore looked for cheaper ways to hold a building together. One is to run horizontal bands of timber or thin concrete through the walls at floor and roof level, tying the corners so that the walls move as a single box rather than as separate slabs. Another is to replace heavy roofs with lighter ones, so that less weight waits overhead. A third is simply to build walls lower and openings smaller.

None of these methods makes a house quake-proof. Their aim is more modest and more realistic: to keep it standing long enough for the people inside to get out. An engineer named Sana, who trained village masons in such techniques, put it plainly. "I can't promise them a house that won't crack," she said. "I can promise them one that won't fall on the people inside."

eng-p096.title: Rubbish in Orbit
eng-p096.text:
Since the first satellites were launched, people have left things behind in space: spent rocket stages, broken satellites, flecks of paint, even a lost tool or two. Most of this debris circles the earth at speeds many times faster than a rifle bullet. At such speeds, a fragment no bigger than a marble carries enough energy to wreck a working satellite, and the wreck itself becomes thousands of new fragments.

This is the worry that keeps space engineers awake. Every collision makes another collision more likely, so that in the busiest orbits debris could, in principle, go on multiplying even if no one launched anything again. Satellites that forecast the weather, guide aircraft and carry telephone calls all depend on those orbits staying usable.

Several remedies are being tried. Many satellites are now designed to burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their working lives, rather than drifting forever. Others are pushed into little-used "graveyard" orbits far from the crowded lanes. Engineers have tested nets, harpoons and magnets for dragging dead satellites down, though none is yet cheap enough to use widely.

The deeper difficulty is not technical but human. Space is shared by many countries and companies, and cleaning it costs money while benefiting everyone, including those who paid nothing. Until those who use space agree on rules and share the bill, the rubbish is likely to keep piling up.

eng-p097.title: The Lift That Cannot Fall
eng-p097.text:
Many people who step into a lift in a tall building feel a small flicker of unease. What if the cable snaps? The fear is understandable, but it rests on a picture of lifts that has been out of date for well over a century.

To begin with, a lift does not hang from a single cable. It is held by several steel ropes, each strong enough to carry the full car on its own, so the chance of all of them failing at once is tiny. Even so, designers do not rely on the ropes alone. Every lift also carries a separate safety device, often called a governor, which watches how fast the car is moving. If the car ever begins to drop faster than a set limit, the governor trips a pair of clamps fitted to the car. These grip the steel rails along which it runs, and the car slows to a firm stop.

The cleverest feature of the design is that it fails safe. The clamps need no electricity to work; they are held open during normal running and snap shut when released. A power cut therefore does not disable the brake. It simply leaves the car where it is.

Lifts can still break down, of course, and a car stuck between floors is no one's idea of fun. But being stuck is a nuisance, not a danger. For most passengers, the real risk in a lift is boredom.

eng-p098.title: Telling a Planet from a Star
eng-p098.text:
Look up on a clear night away from bright lights and a few of the brightest points in the sky will behave differently from the rest. Most will twinkle, flickering and even flashing colours near the horizon. A handful will shine with a steady glow. The steady ones are usually planets, and the difference tells us something about how far away they are.

A star is so distant that, even through a large telescope, it appears as a single point of light. That thin thread of light must pass through many kilometres of moving air, whose pockets of warmer and cooler gas bend it this way and that. Because the beam is so narrow, each tiny bend makes it seem to jump or dim, and we see a twinkle. A planet is far closer. Though it too looks like a dot to the naked eye, it is really a tiny disc, made of countless points of light. Each point is bent by the air, but the bends average out across the disc, and the planet appears to shine steadily.

There is a second test, though it takes patience. Over weeks, a planet slowly changes its position against the background of stars, which keep their patterns from year to year. The old name 'planet', meaning wanderer, records this very habit.

Neither test is perfect. On a night of very turbulent air, even a planet low in the sky may flicker. But together they let anyone with sharp eyes tell a world from a sun.

eng-p099.title: In Defence of Boredom
eng-p099.text:
Ask a teenager in a waiting room what they are doing and the answer, almost always, is something on a phone. The minutes that our grandparents spent staring out of a bus window or lying on a charpai watching the ceiling fan turn have all but vanished, filled by games, videos and messages. We treat boredom as a problem to be solved, and we have never had better tools for solving it.

I want to say a word in boredom's favour. An empty hour is uncomfortable precisely because the mind, given nothing to chew on, starts looking for something. It wanders, recalls, rehearses, and occasionally stumbles on an idea it would never have reached while busy. Many people report that their best thoughts arrive in the shower or on a long walk: places where there is little to do except think. Boredom, in other words, is often the waiting room of imagination.

None of this means we should seek out dullness or throw away our phones. A long, empty day can be grim rather than fruitful, and for someone who is lonely or anxious, distraction can be a kindness. My point is narrower. When we reach for a screen the instant a moment goes quiet, we may be filling the very space in which original thought begins.

So the next time you are kept waiting, try leaving the phone in your pocket for five minutes. Nothing may happen. But something might.

eng-p100.title: Throwing Good Money After Bad
eng-p100.text:
Suppose you have paid five hundred rupees for a film ticket, and half an hour into the film you realise you are bored. Do you stay? Most people do, telling themselves that leaving would waste the money. But the money is gone whether you stay or not. The only real choice is between spending the next ninety minutes bored and spending them on something better.

Economists call money that has already been spent and cannot be recovered a sunk cost, and they warn that it should play no part in decisions about the future. Yet people find this remarkably hard to accept. A family keeps repairing an old car because they have "already put so much into it", though a new one would now cost them less over a year. A company pours more money into a failing project because abandoning it would mean admitting that the earlier spending was a mistake.

The trap is understandable. Walking away feels like losing, and no one likes to look foolish. But the past investment is a reason for regret, not a reason to continue. The sensible question is always the same: knowing what I know now, is the next rupee worth spending?

This does not mean giving up at the first difficulty. Some projects deserve patience, and persistence often pays. The point is to judge them by what lies ahead, not by what has already been poured in.

eng-p101.title: Why We Put Things Off
eng-p101.text:
Hamza had a week to write his history essay. On Monday he tidied his desk. On Tuesday he reorganised the files on his computer. By Thursday evening his room had never been cleaner, and the essay had not been started.

Hamza is not lazy; he worked hard all week, just not at the essay. People who study putting things off have reached a surprising conclusion: it is less a problem of managing time than of managing feelings. A task that makes us anxious, or bored, or afraid of doing badly, produces an unpleasant feeling, and avoiding the task makes the feeling go away at once. The relief is immediate; the cost arrives later. Small wonder the habit is so stubborn.

If that is the cause, then the usual advice, to make a stricter timetable, misses the point. A timetable tells us when to start but does nothing about the dread. Some simpler tricks work better. One is to shrink the first step until it seems almost silly: not 'write the essay' but 'write one sentence'. Another is to be kind to oneself after a slip, since people who forgive themselves for delaying once seem less likely to delay again.

Hamza, in the end, wrote his first sentence at ten on Thursday night. It was not a good sentence. But it was a start, and by midnight he had a page.

eng-p102.title: Growing Up with Two Languages
eng-p102.text:
In many Pakistani homes a child hears one language from her grandmother, another from her friends and a third in her textbooks. Parents sometimes worry that this mixture will confuse her, and that she would be better off mastering one language properly before touching another.

The worry is natural, but it is largely misplaced. Children who grow up with two or more languages do sometimes mix words from both in a single sentence, and they may take a little longer to build a large vocabulary in each. These are not signs of confusion. A child who borrows an Urdu word in the middle of an English sentence usually knows exactly what she is doing: she is reaching for the word that comes to mind first, as adults who speak two languages do all the time.

Meanwhile, managing two languages appears to bring quiet advantages. A bilingual child must constantly choose which language to use with whom, and keep the other from slipping in. Many researchers believe this daily practice in switching and holding back strengthens the mind's control over attention. Bilingual children also learn early that the same thing can be named in different ways, a small but real insight into how language works.

None of this makes a second language a magic key to cleverness, and a child still needs rich, patient conversation in at least one language to thrive. But a home full of languages is not a burden to be managed. It is a gift.

eng-p103.title: Quiet Voices in Loud Rooms
eng-p103.text:
In most group discussions, the first idea spoken aloud gets the most attention, and the people who speak first are usually the most confident, not always the most thoughtful. Anyone who has sat through a class project knows the pattern: two or three voices fill the room, and the rest nod along.

Teachers and managers often read this as a simple difference between talkers and thinkers, but it is better seen as a difference in how people prefer to work. Some think best out loud. They need to hear an idea spoken before they can judge it, and a lively argument sharpens them. Others think best in silence. They want to turn a problem over alone before offering a view, and by the time they are ready, the group has often moved on. Neither style is superior; each catches mistakes that the other misses.

The trouble is that most meetings are designed for the first kind of person. A simple change can restore the balance. If everyone writes down their ideas privately for five minutes before anyone speaks, the quiet thinkers arrive at the discussion with something ready, and the early speakers can no longer set the direction alone. Some groups also share the agenda a day in advance, giving their more reflective members time to prepare.

The point is not to silence the talkers. It is to make sure a group hears from everyone it has gathered, rather than only from those who are quickest to speak.

eng-p104.title: The Song You Cannot Stop Humming
eng-p104.text:
Almost everyone has had the experience: a few bars of a tune, heard once on the radio or at a wedding, refuse to leave. They play over and over for hours, sometimes days, often at the least convenient moments. Researchers who study these 'earworms' have found that they are very common, and that the tunes involved tend to share certain features.

The tunes that stick are usually simple, with a clear rhythm and a melody that rises and falls in a pattern the ear can predict, yet with one small surprise, an unexpected note or a skipped beat, that catches the attention. Repetition helps; a chorus heard many times is more likely to return than a song heard once. Oddly, it is often a fragment rather than a whole song that sticks: a few lines that stop without resolving.

That last feature offers a clue to why earworms happen at all. The mind seems to dislike leaving things unfinished. A fragment that stops in the middle is like a question without an answer, and the brain keeps replaying it, as if trying to complete it. This would also explain a piece of folk advice that some people swear by: listen to the whole song through to the end, and the loop is more likely to stop.

Earworms are rarely harmful, and most fade within a day. But they offer a small window into how the mind treats the unfinished, a habit that reaches well beyond music.

eng-p105.title: After the Last Guest Leaves
eng-p105.text:
Anyone who has attended a large wedding in Pakistan knows the scene near midnight: long tables still crowded with dishes of rice and curry, half-eaten plates stacked high, and staff scraping food into bins. Hosts, anxious that no guest should ever find an empty dish, order far more than can be eaten. Generosity, in this case, ends in waste.

It is easy to blame hosts, but they are caught in a custom that punishes moderation. A family that orders exactly enough risks the shame of running out, and that shame lasts longer in memory than any number of full bins. No single family can change the custom alone.

Some groups have begun to tackle the problem from the other end. In several towns, volunteers arrange with caterers to collect untouched food at the end of an event, pack it safely and deliver it the same night to shelters and to families in need. The key word is untouched: food that has sat on a guest's plate cannot be passed on, so the work depends on caterers setting the surplus aside before it is served. Other organisers encourage hosts to serve smaller portions, with second helpings on request, so that less food is heaped onto plates and abandoned.

These efforts will not end waste on their own. But they show that hospitality and good sense need not be enemies. A wedding can still be generous; it simply needs a plan for what happens after the last guest leaves.

eng-p106.title: The Chess Club in Room Nine
eng-p106.text:
I joined the chess club in Room Nine because my friend Danish had joined it, and I expected to be good at chess within a week. I had beaten my younger cousins many times. On my first afternoon, a thin, quiet girl from the class below mine, Mehwish, beat me in eleven moves. I asked for another game. She beat me in nine.

For a month I lost to nearly everyone. I began to dread Thursday afternoons and to invent reasons to leave early. What kept me coming, I think, was Mehwish herself. After each game she would set the pieces back to where my position had fallen apart and ask, without a trace of mockery, 'What were you hoping would happen here?' Usually I had no answer. I had been moving pieces, not making plans.

Slowly I learned to ask myself her question before each move. I still lost, but the games grew longer, and I began to see my mistakes a move or two before they cost me. In March I drew a game against Danish, and walking home that day I felt as if the road were tilting downhill.

I never became very good. But I took something from Room Nine that I have used far more often than any chess opening: the habit of stopping, before I act, to ask what I am actually hoping will happen.

eng-p107.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
eng-p107.text:
The power went at half past eight, during the worst of the June heat, and this time it did not come back after the usual hour. By ten our flat had become an oven. My father opened every window, which let in nothing but more heat and the sound of a hundred other families doing the same.

It was my mother who suggested the roof. We carried up a jug of water, a pile of cushions and the old battery torch, and found that we were not the first. The Siddiquis from the third floor had already spread a mat. Mrs Baig, who had lived below us for six years and to whom I had perhaps said ten words, arrived with a plate of sliced mangoes and an apology for having nothing more.

Nobody planned what followed. Someone's uncle told a long, improbable story about a buffalo that had followed him home from a market. Children who had only ever nodded at each other on the stairs began a game of hide-and-seek among the water tanks. Mrs Baig, it turned out, had once been a singer, and when asked shyly, she sang.

The power returned a little after two. Fans whirred back to life below, and one by one the families gathered their things and went down. The next morning the building was itself again, everyone hurrying to work and school. But Mrs Baig and my mother now drink tea together every Sunday, and when I pass the Siddiqui boys on the stairs, we stop to talk.

eng-p108.title: The Letter on the Doorstep
eng-p108.text:
When I was fifteen I broke the side window of Mr Qureshi's car with a cricket ball. It was an accident, a wild shot that flew off the edge of my bat, but I did not stay to explain. I ran, and so did my friends, and for three days I waited for a knock on our door that never came.

It was the silence that wore me down. Mr Qureshi had covered the window with plastic, and every morning I watched him peel it back, check the seat for rain and drive off to work. He did not look angry. He looked tired. On the fourth evening I sat down and wrote him a letter. I tore up the first two drafts, which were full of excuses about the wind and the uneven ground, and in the third I simply said what I had done and that I would pay for the glass.

I delivered it myself, which took more courage than writing it. He read it on his doorstep while I stood there, and then, to my surprise, he laughed. He said he had known it was me all along; he had seen me from his kitchen window. He had been waiting, he said, to see whether I would come.

I paid for the glass over four months from my pocket money. It was the most expensive lesson of my childhood, and the cheapest.

eng-p109.title: The Art of Not Being Seen
eng-p109.text:
For an animal that is hunted, the best defence is often not to be noticed at all. Camouflage, the art of blending in, takes several forms, and each works by fooling the eye in a slightly different way.

The simplest is matching the background. A desert lark is the colour of sand and stones; a green grasshopper vanishes among leaves. But colour alone is rarely enough, because a hunter's eye is quick to spot an outline. Many animals therefore break up their shape with bold patches or stripes. A leopard's spots, which seem eye-catching in a zoo, scatter its outline among the shadows of a forest floor until the animal's edges seem to dissolve.

A subtler trick deals with light. In sunlight, an animal's back is lit and its belly is in shadow, and this contrast makes it look solid and round, easy to pick out. Many fish, deer and birds are darker on top and paler underneath. The pale belly cancels the shadow, and the body appears flat, almost as though it were part of the scene.

Some creatures go further still. Certain octopuses can alter both the colour and the texture of their skin in moments, turning from smooth and pale against sand to rough and mottled against rock. Yet all these methods share one limit: they work best when the animal keeps still. Movement, more than colour or shape, is what most often gives a hidden creature away.

eng-p110.title: My Grandfather's Clay Pot
eng-p110.text:
When I was eleven, my grandfather gave me a clay money pot with a slit in the top and no way to open it except by breaking it. 'Put in something every week,' he said, 'even if it is only a coin. Don't count it. Don't shake it. Break it when you need something that matters.'

I thought it was a dull present. Coins were small, and a week of them would buy almost nothing. For the first months I fed it only when I remembered, and I shook it constantly, trying to guess the total from the rattle. Then the rattle stopped, which meant the pot was too full for the coins to move, and something shifted in me. I began dropping in a note now and then, then every Friday, without quite deciding to.

Nearly three years later, my bicycle was stolen from outside the school. My parents could not easily afford another, and I was too proud to ask. I broke the pot on the kitchen floor. Among the pieces lay more money than I had ever held, enough for a second-hand bicycle and a lock.

What surprised me was not the amount but how little I had felt each addition. No single coin had been a sacrifice. My grandfather, I realised, had not given me a pot at all. He had given me a habit, and the pot was only the excuse.
